The house resumed, from Friday, February 24, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe (Port Arthur):
That a special committee be appointed to examine into the role of government in the field of nonmilitary research in Canada, including:
(a)	operations in the field of atomic energy,
(b)	operations of the national research council.
That the committee be empowered to sit during
the sittings of the house and to print such papers and evidence from day to day as may be ordered by the committee and to report from time to time; and that notwithstanding standing order No. 67 the committee shall consist of 20 members.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. H. Dickey (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subsubtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN NON-MILITARY RESEARCH
speechtext:
The
purpose of this resolution is disclosed by its terms as they appear on the order paper. It
Committee on Atomic Energy is to set up a special committee of this house to consider the role of the federal government in non-military research in Canada. In making this study the committee is expected to review the operations of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and of the national research council, and to consider also research in its general aspects.
In previous sessions committees of a similar nature were set up. The first was in 1949, and that committee was known as the committee on atomic energy. In 1950 we established a sessional committee on the operations of the national research council.
In 1953 we had a second committee on atomic energy. All of these committees, Mr. Speaker, did valuable work. However, during the last several years considerable changes have occurred in the organization of the atomic energy project and in its relations to the national research council. Further study by a committee of this house of the activities of the government in both these fields seems to be appropriate at this session. The operations of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and of research laboratories are quite complicated, and a committee of this house gives the members an opportunity to appreciate the problems involved and to obtain much more detailed information on these matters than would otherwise be possible.
There is no question that after the previous committees had met the members of this house had a much better appreciation of what was involved. It is also true that the last five years have brought about an increasing interest in research on the part of hon. members. This has been indicated by a wider variety of questions asked and in particular by the interest in the debate two years ago on the amendments to the national Research Council Act. At that time the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) made a full statement about the operations of the national research council, and accordingly I do not propose to go into any detail today. I would, however, like to point out certain changes which have occurred in the administration and operation of the national research council and in general government support of academic and industrial research.

speechtext:
The major changes which have occurred in the organization since 1950 are, first the setting up of Atomic Energy of

Committee on Atomic Energy Canada Limited as a crown company in 1952 . and the transfer to it from the national research council of responsibility for work on atomic energy. The company has now been in existence for four years, and our experience shows that the new arrangement has been entirely successful. In addition, the fact that the president of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited is also the president-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, the hon. member is speaking louder but there is a good deal of talking in his general area. This important statement the hon. member is making should be appreciated by all if hon. members around him would speak a little more softly.

subsubtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN NON-MILITARY RESEARCH
speechtext: If he would hold the speech up a little and speak out.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subsubtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN NON-MILITARY RESEARCH
speechtext:
The president of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited is also the president of Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited, and this has meant a consolidation of activities connected with atomic energy, including both research in the atomic field and the production of uranium.
In spite of the necessity of separating Atomic Energy of Canada Limited from the national research council, co-operation between those two bodies has remained extremely close.
The other main change since 1950 has been the completion of several buildings and division of the national research council which were under way at the time of the first committee. The maritime regional laboratory, which was under construction then, is now in full operation.
The division of building research has now a building of its own and has been expanded to something like full size. The division of radio and electrical engineering is now housed in its own building on the Montreal road and the division of applied chemistry has been expanded and also now has its own building.
As far as research in general is concerned, there has been a very considerable increase in activity and interest in the last five years. With reference to government research, I shall not enlarge on the position since it was dealt with during the past two sessions of parliament, except to say that at the present time $70 million per annum is being spent by the federal government on research. I think that one can say with justice that the per capita expenditure on government research in Canada of a nonmilitary nature is now on a level where it compares favourably with any country in the world.
Further, I think that one can well be proud of the quality of the work which is 'Mr. Dickey.]

being done in various government organizations. A considerable expansion has also taken place in government support to university research. As far as the national research council is concerned, this increase has been a dramatic one, the amount rising from a few thousand dollars at the end of the first war to something like $2J million today. In particular university support by the national research council has multiplied by a factor of about five since the end of the second war. There is no question that support from the national research council over the years has been a major factor in the development of university research in Canada.
I should also like to say something about industrial research in which there has been an increasing interest and activity over the past few years. We are at a stage in this country in our industrial development where we must to a greater and greater extent think for ourselves along technical lines. There is a very satisfactory trend in this direction which must be continued. The only way, however, in which industrial research can really develop is on the basis of appreciation by industry that it is necessary. All that the government can do in this regard is to make tax concessions to try to take care through government laboratories of the smaller industries and to help the larger industries in the transition period before they get their own research going, to advise and encourage and to set the example by operating first-rate laboratories itself.
I believe that the Canadian picture in industrial research is encouraging. We have developed research in the federal government to a stage where we can be thoroughly proud of the results. Most provincial governments have also become interested in research with a provincial outlook. Our industries are becoming research conscious and we are giving them every possible encouragement from the point of view of taxation. All in all, I think we are on the right track and the future of Canadian research should be a bright one. However, since we are in a transition period it appears to be an excellent time for a committee of this house to look into the whole question of the status of Canadian governmental research.

subsubtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN NON-MILITARY RESEARCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in opening my remarks I should like to reread the terms of the resolution which are as follows:
That a special committee be appointed to examine into the role of government in the field of nonmilitary research in Canada, including:
(a)	operations in the field of atomic energy,
(b)	operations of the national research council.
That the committee be empowered to sit during
the sittings of the house and to print such papers and evidence from day to day as may be ordered

by the committee and to report from time to time; and that notwithstanding standing order No. 67 the committee shall consist of twenty members.
There are some features of that resolution which I think deserve further consideration. One is that in effect it calls for two inquiries, one into the field of atomic energy and the other into the operations of the national research council. The official opposition support the idea of having these two fields investigated, but we believe it would have been wiser to have separate committees. After all there is a great deal to be considered in each of the fields and during the discussion of this question last session the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated that he believed that there should be two committees rather than one.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN NON-MILITARY RESEARCH
speechtext:
Oh, no. Can my
hon. friend quote me on that?

subsubtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN NON-MILITARY RESEARCH
speechtext:
Yes, certainly. At page 6215 of Hansard for July 15, 1955, the Minister of Trade and Commerce is reported as follows;
Next year we shall be very glad to consider It.
There had been discussion about a committee.
I think it is better to have a committee on atomic energy. I believe it is a big enough field.
If other committees in the fields of science are needed, perhaps they could be separate committees.
A second feature of this motion is that it takes out of the scope of the committee the field of military research. I believe the government was correct in not asking this committee to investigate that field, but I suggest that the field of military research is one in which an investigation might save the country a great deal of money. At the present time large sums of money are being spent in this field and there is an increase in the estimates for the current year. Yet parliament has practically no way of checking these particular expenditures.
The other features of this motion to which I should like to refer is that there is severe restriction upon the powers of the committee in that it will not be allowed to send for persons and papers. If hon. members will look at the order paper they will see that Item No. 9 is a motion to set up a committee to consider the work of the federal district commission and that committee is to have the power to send for persons and papers. Item No. 13 covers a motion to set up a committee to consider certain aspects of the criminal law of Canada, which committee is also to be given the power to send for persons and papers. The last item on the order paper is a motion to set up a committee on the Canadian National Railways and Trans-Canada Air Lines. That committee also
Committee on Atomic Energy is given the power to send for persons, papers and records. We believe that the committee on atomic energy and research should be given the same powers. It is my purpose before I sit down to move an amendment to that effect. I hope the government will consider such amendment on its merits.
We believe that this committee is a very important one. In earlier years when there has been a committee on atomic energy the members have acted in a responsible and conscientious way, and I am sure they will do the same thing this year. I know that the Minister of Trade and Commerce would agree with those remarks. I do not believe there has ever been a better committee of the house than the committees that have been set up to consider the question of atomic energy and the operations of the national research council.
Today I propose to deal only with the atomic energy field. The other field, namely, the operations of the national research council, will be dealt with in the first place by my colleague, the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy). In so far as the atomic energy field is concerned, we are not satisfied with the position of parliament. It is quite significant that in making the opening speech in this debate today the parliamentary assistant barely mentioned the atomic energy field. Most of his remarks had to do with the national research council.
I do not intend to belittle the work of that council because we have great admiration for the work it has done. I simply point out that the government itself in its opening statement today has given the house practically no information with regard to the atomic energy field. That indicates very clearly the point I wish to make, that we do not believe parliament is in its proper position with regard to the atomic energy field.
In the first place, there is almost a complete lack of information given to the house about what is happening in this particular field. It is true that each year certain estimates are passed which deal with atomic energy activities but the questioning during the discussion of those estimates is of necessity of a very desultory nature. It is quite impossible to gather much information in that way, and parliament, and beyond parliament, the people, have been getting very little information about what is going on in Canada in this field.
On two occasions there has been a special committee of the house on atomic energy, the first being in 1949. It was only set up after years of pleading by members of all three

Committee on Atomic Energy opposition parties. The original Atomic Energy Control Act was passed in 1946 and at that time, leading off tor the Conservative party, I urged as earnestly as I could that there should be a committee of the house on atomic energy. That request was not granted. Finally, three years later in 1949 the first special committee was set up.
That committee found that the field was so wide and so important that it recommended that a committee be se up in the following year. I have here the recommendation of the 1949 committee which is as follows:
Your committee has been in existence for only six weeks and in that time has been unable to complete its examination into the field of atomic energy development. Furthermore, this field is a new one, is widening rapidly, and may well be of tremendous importance to Canada. For these reasons your committee recommends that a special committee be reconstituted next session.
The recommendation made by the 1949 committee is still a valid and sound recommendation because as we know the field has been widening steadily in the meantime and much more rapidly than anyone expected in 1949. However, the government would not set up a committee again in 1950 and we did not succeed in getting the second committee until the year 1953.
1 believe that what is needed is a standing committee of the house on atomic energy. As things are at present, the Minister of Trade and Commerce alone knows what is going on in this field. His parliamentary assistant may have some information. The hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr, Mcllraith), who was chairman of the special committee in 1949 and also in 1953, I believe, may have some knowledge. But essentially the only member of the parliament of Canada today who has any detailed knowledge of the atomic energy field is the Minister of Trade and Commerce himself. I make no comments today about its being that particular minister but I think this is an unsound situation to exist in the parliament of Canada.
This field is much too important to have the detailed knowledge concerning it possessed by only one person. The United States has gone at this particular problem of keeping the elected bodies in touch with the atomic energy field in a different way. I realize that their governmental system differs greatly from our own, but in this particular respect I think we could very well copy at least a portion of the organization they have set up. They have three watchdog committees over atomic energy. One is made up of defence people, a second of scientists appointed from all over the United States, and the third is the congressional committee, a joint committee which is really the congressional

watchdog committee on atomic energy. Their job is to make continual studies of the development of atomic energy and to keep congress fully acquainted with such developments.
I understand they actually have a permanent staff, and right from the start they have been in very close touch with what has gone on in the United States in the atomic energy field. I see no reason why, under our parliamentary system, we should not have a standing committee on atomic energy. I admit that the problem is a difficult one. I am not trying to be partisan at all in these remarks. I admit it is a difficult problem to meet, but I believe that one of the best ways of keeping the membership of the House of Commons informed on what is happening in this field and also of keeping Canadian newspapers and the Canadian people informed would be by having a standing committee.
At one time we met the explanation or the excuse that there was so much secret information in the atomic energy field that it would not be possible to have any such committee. I have here a statement made by the classification officer of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited since this house has been sitting. I am quoting from a dispatch from Chalk River on January 31, 1956, by John Bird. It is a Canadian Press dispatch. In it we find these statements:
Officials of A.E.C. were emphatic in saying that all the atomic information necessary for development work on power stations is available to private industry. Statements to the effect that secrecy considerations impeded the release of such information were termed incorrect.
"There is a mistaken impression that atomic energy for peaceful uses still is hush-hush," said Dr. G. O. Baines, classification officer for A.E.C. "Very little now is secret at Chalk River and other atomic plants not engaged in weapon production."
I believe that industry in Canada now knows far more about the atomic energy field than do members of parliament themselves. Mr. Speaker, parliament simply must be brought into this picture, for several reasons. One is this. It is a new field. This atomic energy field is the most important new field in Canada in the lifetime of any member of this house. There has never been a more important field opened up in the lifetime of anyone in this house today. It is a most important field in war. By reason of the development of atomic energy we were able to win the war in the Pacific in short order. By the same token we might very well have lost the war just as rapidly if the Germans had achieved this development before the allies. It is a most important field in peacetime as well. New questions are raised. There is need for new policies; and the responsibility for those new policies, in the final analysis, is not on the government of

Canada but on the parliament of Canada. How can the parliament of Canada accept that responsibility if it is not informed of what is going on in this field? I point out to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) that the government must be extremely careful to keep parliament informed of the developments in this field.
Another reason is this. Now that power is being produced from atomic energy, where and how is it to be used? That is one of the problems that should be faced by this parliament. Last summer there was a conference at Geneva. It was the first international conference on the peaceful uses of atomic energy. Canada was represented and the members of parliament of Canada, by reading the newspapers, learned what the Canadian officials had to say about this field. I have here a dispatch from Geneva dated August 8, 1955. This was all information that could have been given to the parliament of Canada last session. There should have been discussion about the matter here on the floor of the house. I am quoting from a report of a paper read by Dr. John Davis of the minister's own department. By the way, I believe that Dr. Davis is one of the outstanding men in the service of this country today. This report states as follows:
He said-
That is referring to Dr. Davis.
-as many as ten atomic power stations each capable of generating up to 100,000 kilowatts of electric energy, may be required in Canada in the late 1960's or early 1970's.
Dr. Davis told the conference the majority of the plants probably will be located in southern Ontario.
This is important information to people from all over Canada.
Others may be needed in the maritimes and possibly in southern Manitoba.
Dr. Davis also said a larger number of nuclear power plants with a generating capacity of from 2,000 to 3,000 kilowatts could make a more modest contribution to Canada's energy requirements.
They would likely be required in the north country and by industries such as pulp and paper which could use both the power and the by-product heat.
Then there were further reports of the statements made by Canadians at Geneva. I have here another dispatch two days later, on August 10, 1955, in which we find this statement:
The Canadian paper-
That is the official government paper, presumably.
-said that between 1960 and 1970, an increasing number of thermal plants under construction in Canada will be of the nuclear variety.
It said a ratio of one to one in the construction of new nuclear and other thermal plants at that period "would mark the beginning of an entirely
Committee on Atomic Energy
new era-that of the emergence of atomic power as a major, if not the major, source of electricity in Canada."
It is obvious that this atomic power is mobile. It can be carried to different parts of the country. Again, since this house has been in session, we have had a dispatch indicating that atomic power will probably be used at a power station on an Arctic island to generate power for signals between the northern radar chains. Just about ten days ago Mr. W. J. Bennett, the president of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, was quoted as follows:
Mr. Bennett said that Chalk River scientists are considering design studies for a small reactor which would supply power and space heating in remote areas of northern Canada where the cost of conventional thermal fuels is excessive.
Development of such a reactor would make possible a vast reduction in northern costs. Fuel now is transported to outposts at a cost ranging to 9100 a ton. With adequate heating supplies vegetables now imported at great expense could be grown in glass houses far within the Arctic circle.
Northern Affairs officials look forward to construction in such small reactors as a major contribution to the extension of the boundaries of settlement.
Then another reason that this field is of such great importance is this. A large segment of the mining industry of Canada is now directly involved in the atomic energy field. I refer to the mining of uranium ore. Fortunately Canada has large uranium ore resources. We are one of the most fortunate nations in the world in that regard. That is one reason why we should always be in the forefront in this particular field. But the mining of uranium ore is not like the mining of lead and zinc ore in my old home district of Kootenay in British Columbia or in the other mining districts of Canada. While the mining of those ores is under provincial control, the mining of uranium ore is under the control of the dominion.
It is under drastic federal control exercised I believe through a crown company, Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited. There are regulations for the mining of this ore. It can only be sold to that crown company. A smelter cannot buy uranium ore without the consent of Eldorado. Furthermore, Eldorado is the sole processor in Canada of uranium ore. This field of mining uranium has expanded in a tremendous way. I have here the latest report of the atomic energy control board of Canada for the fiscal year 1954-55. We find on page 9, under the heading "Prospecting and Mining", the following:
Several events combined to make the year under review very significant for uranium mining. Production was larger than in any previous year because it was the first in which the plant of

Committee on Atomic Energy
Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited at Beaver-lodge in northern Saskatchewan was in operation for a full year. Also, for the first time, production at this plant was augmented by ore shipped to it from private properties in the district. In addition, contracts for large production from one property in Saskatchewan, and three in the Blind River district of Ontario were negotiated and production from these is expected to begin shortly. The scale of these operations is indicated by the fact that the purchase price of concentrates to be delivered under these contracts totals over $338 million. Promising results were obtained at several other properties in fairly advanced stages of exploration.
This report is over a year old and I have no doubt that the situation is even better at the present time. The report also has this to say:
Prospectors were active in almost all provinces and territories and more persons were searching for uranium than for any other metal, and many new discoveries were reported.
Then there is a report dated October 27, 1955, in which Mr. Bennett is quoted as predicting that Canada would be producing $180 million worth of uranium in 1958, making it the third ranking metal in gross dollar value in the Canadian production picture. As I pointed out, here is a mining field in which the dominion government is supreme and members of parliament should know all about the uranium policy of this government. Having been given that knowledge, they should be in a position to make suggestions as to ways in which that policy could be improved. I need only point out the great confusion that last year followed upon certain statements by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, then by the Prime Minister, and then again by the Minister of Trade and Commerce with regard to the uranium policy of this government.
Another reason why this is of such importance to parliament is that the development of the Northwest Territories is involved. It was in that area, at Great Bear lake, that the first mine was developed, and Eldorado, through its subsidiary known as Northern Transportation Company Limited, has a very important part in the opening up of northern Canada. We have had some rather bitter complaints from residents of the Northwest Territories about the rates charged by this crown company in northern transportation. I have here a dispatch dated November 27, 1955, reporting representations made before the Gordon economic commission concerning what were alleged to be these outrageous charges levied by this crown company for transportation in the north.
The report says:
Spokesmen for one community-the famed goldmining town of Yellowknife-charged that the federal air transport policy is bankrupt and that

a federal crown company operating in the north is making fantastic profits on water shipping.
The article goes on:
But all agreed that the most urgent need is for more transportation facilities and a reduction of high shipping charges.
. . . While discussion centred on the rail line, Yellowknife emphasized that much could be done to reduce shipping tolls by reassessing federal policy.
A federal crown company, Northern Transportation, was making exorbitant profits-about 350 per cent on the federal investment-in water shipments on the Great Slave lake and Mackenzie river routes.
"It is hard to believe," said Yellowknife's spokesmen, "that the federal cabinet is aware of the exorbitant profits which its own company is extracting from the relatively few people who live in the Mackenzie river area. We do not believe that the people of Canada as a whole would condone this exploitation.
Now, that statement may have been exaggerated, but in any event this question of transportation in northern Canada is under the control of a crown corporation operating in this atomic energy field, and that particular question should also be very carefully investigated by the parliament of Canada.
Another reason in support of my submission that parliament should be put much more fully into this picture is the amount of money that is involved. This atomic energy development in Canada has already taken a great many millions of dollars of the taxpayers money, and it is taking more every year. Parliament votes the money and should know all the facts before this money is voted. I believe that in the last four years parliament has voted something like $120 million for this purpose. The votes for this year, as I estimate them, aggregate something over $36 million.
Last year the Minister of Trade and Commerce under questioning about the expenditures told me, as reported at page 6215 of Hansard for July 15, 1955, the figure for this current fiscal year 1956-57 would be $34,066,000. As I say, the estimate now introduced is at least $2 million higher and no doubt there will be supplementary estimates. He said:
It goes down. This is a big year; $34,006,000 next year; 1957, $31 million;-
I am not sure from the figures whether the minister was referring to last year or this coming fiscal year. I took it originally he had in mind that the expenditure for 1956-57 would be $31 million, but no matter which of these figures is correct the expenditures are very heavy. Parliament has a responsibility to examine much more fully than it has done in the past into these figures. We should have an effective check on the expenditure, and there is no such check at the present time. Take, for example, the new

N.R.U. reactor. When the announcement was first made that it was to be built we were told the cost would be $30 million. Last year the minister said at page 6155 of Hansard that the cost would be between $35 and $40 million. This year we read in the papers that the cost is now up to $50 million. I hold in my hand a dispatch from the Vancouver Sun dated December 8, 1955, which says: Atomic pile cost now $50 million Chalk River, Ontario.
Cost of the N.R.U. atomic energy reactor has been boosted a second time by $10 million.
Whether those figures are accurate is beside the point. The fact is, the reactor is going to cost many millions of dollars more than parliament was told it would cost in the beginning.
Another reason why parliament should go much more fully into this field is in connection with what is happening today. Today in Paris the nations are meeting to set up what is known as the international atomic energy agency.

subsubtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN NON-MILITARY RESEARCH
speechtext:
Just last week President Eisenhower signed an order committing 85,000 pounds of uranium 235 to peaceful purposes over the next forty years, thereby clearing the way for huge financing operations to build nuclear power plants in those parts of the world that are not able to build them themselves. The reports indicate that at least $1 billion worth of nuclear fuel would be available for sale or release to private power stations during that period.
Canada from the start has been one of the nations in the lead in the atomic energy field. I think it is very praiseworthy that we are helping to establish this international agency. The purpose, of course, is to spread peaceful atomic knowledge as widely as possible in the world and to work out the allocation of reactors and atomic fuel for the nations that are not fortunate enough to be able to develop these particular things themselves. Here again Canada is stepping into this broader aspect of the atomic energy field and parliament should have a chance to keep informed at all times about those developments.
For the reasons I have outlined, Mr. Speaker, the official opposition urge that this
Committee on Atomic Energy committee, which is to be set up this year, be given very wide powers and great latitude. The members of the committee should be taken to Chalk River, and also be given the opportunity to visit Beaverlodge in northern Saskatchewan and the refinery at Port Hope. They should inquire into the activities of all governmental agencies, the atomic energy control board, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited, and Northern Transportation Company Limited. In addition, they should be given a thorough explanation of the government's uranium policy and be put in a position where they can make recommendations which would lead to the promotion and the better control of the mining of uranium in Canada.
Then, another very important question which they should be allowed to consider is the extent to which Canada can stand on her own feet in this field. I pointed out earlier that we have the uranium and that we started out with the leading nations, United States and Great Britain. It does seem of great importance that we be able to stand on our own feet. For example, we are not yet able to process fully our own uranium ore. I hold in my hand the report of Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited for the calendar year 1954. On page 7 I find:
As indicated in previous reports, the operation of the new refining circuit will permit the company to produce a purified or metal grade product.
They are referring, of course, to the Port Hope plant. I continue:
This is an essential step towards the production of uranium metal in Canada.
Last year Mr. Bennett said he anticipated that Canada might soon be in a position to carry out all three stages of uranium processing at its Port Hope plant, thus ending the necessity of exporting it to the United States to finish the product for use in our own reactors. In the press this week I find a warning given in Vancouver by Professor G. M. Volkoff of the University of British Columbia that Canada could find herself buying back her own uranium in the future in the form of complete power units manufactured in England or in the United States. He was speaking to a natural resources conference in Vancouver and he said:
Now is the time for Canada to manufacture and export complete nuclear power plants to the rest of power-hungry world.
We cannot be too careful to adopt policies in this country which will enable us to process our own raw materials in Canada to the greatest extent possible. I hope that in this atomic energy field we are not going to get in the same position we are in in some of the

Committee on Atomic Energy others, such as the iron ore field and others I could mention, under which we dig out the ore and let it go to the United States and buy back the finished product which has been made by the people of the United States.
Another aspect of this question where we think Canada should stand on her own feet in this field is in the production of heavy water. All of our atomic energy reactors at Chalk River use heavy water as a moderator. I have been a member of the two atomic energy committees which have been set up. I visited Chalk River on each occasion, and I call on the other members who served on that committee to endorse my statement that we were told on each occasion the heavy water for Chalk River was produced at Trail, British Columbia. We were told that the plant had been installed by the United States atomic energy commission. There was not any doubt of that; but we were told that the heavy water came from Trail. That statement has been made time and again in the intervening years. I have four or five press dispatches confirming it. One appeared in the Ottawa Journal of May 19, 1954, which reads:
Since Canada entered the atomic energy field her experience has been with experimental reactors partly controlled or moderated with heavy water produced at the Trail, British Columbia, smelter plant.
The next dispatch is dated January 25, 1955, and it appears in the Journal again. It reported a speech by Mr. Bennett. It refers to the new reactor, and reads as follows:
The experimental reactor would use heavy water, produced at Trail, British Columbia, as a moderator or control agent and possibly also to cool the plant.
A press dispatch dated April 27, 1955, which also appeared in the Journal, reads in part as follows:
Heavy water, produced at Trail, B.C., smelter now costs between $720,000 and $1,200,000 a ton. This must be cut because the demand by 1970 is expected to be several hundred tons a year. Methods also must be found to speed output, now about six tons a year from Trail.
An article appeared in the Vancouver Province dated December 9, 1955, written by John E. Bird, reporting on the NRU reactor, which reads in part as follows:
N.R.U. will use heavy water to moderate or slow down the activity of the reactor and to keep it from generating too much heat and melting the fuel rods.
. .	. Heavy water is produced by a highlytechnical electrolytic process at the smelter plant at Trail, B.C., at a cost of about $60 a pound. N.R.U. will contain 43 tons valued at more than $5,000,000.

I also have here a report entitled "Canada's Atomic Energy Project" issued under the minister's own name in March 1953. We find at page 326 a description of the early difficulties in setting up the atomic energy plant. It says:
. . . but of greater importance to the Montreal laboratory was its dependence at that time-
These are the significant words:
-on the United States for the manufacture of heavy water and the reduction of Canadian uranium to the form of metal.
Yet this year when dispatches appeared reporting that the plant at Trail was to be closed down the minister told this house, and I am quoting from page 833 of Hansard:
The government of Canada has never had any interest in the plant nor has it obtained any material from that plant.
I questioned him, pointing out what we had been told when we were serving on the atomic energy committee, and he confirmed his earlier statement. He said, as reported at page 834 of Hansard:
I am surprised that the hon. member has been told that the heavy water at Chalk river came from Trail because it is not to my knowledge that that is the case. We purchase our heavy water from the atomic energy commission of the United States and it is my understanding that it comes from quite a different source.
The point I wish to make is simply that in the first place there should not have been that misunderstanding. Somebody obviously was wrong. I do not know whether the minister was wrong in the statement he made last month or whether the information given to us down through the years was wrong.

speechtext:
Perhaps the minister will be able to explain why there is this difference. I do not, however, wish to deal particularly with the difference in the statements. What I am getting at is the possibility of Canada producing heavy water herself.
We also urge that provision be made for a permanent atomic energy committee of this house and also that every hon. member of

the house should be given the opportunity of visiting the plant at Chalk River. I am sure that suggestion will meet the support of all hon. members who have not yet been there. I think it would be very beneficial to the nation as a whole if all hon. members of parliament who are not to serve on this committee were to be given the chance of going to Chalk River to see what is actually being done there.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would point out that Canada having been in the forefront in the atomic energy field must stay there. It is a wonderful opportunity for this nation. I believe there has been nothing of more importance in recent times in so far as the development of the nation is concerned. In fact, if there is proper leadership and proper activity in this field it can do a great deal to make Canada one of the greatest nations in the world. But that can only be done, Mr. Speaker, if parliament is kept informed and is kept in this picture. That in effect is the essence of my plea today, that parliament be put right in this picture and be kept in this picture throughout.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy):
That the motion be amended by inserting after the word "house" in the sixth line thereof the following:
"to send for persons and unclassified papers and records."

subsubtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN NON-MILITARY RESEARCH
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that I think the minister or the government will have to give a very good explanation as to why the authority to send for persons, papers and records was left out. It may be that there are reasons connected with the atomic energy development which require a certain amount of secrecy. That may be a valid reason, but as I say I think a very strong reason will have to be given to the house; otherwise I think the house should vote for the amendment just moved.
I find it difficult to understand why the house has been denied this right when the resolutions for other committees which have been set up contain such a provision. There may be a special reason in this case, but I think we should be told what the reason is if one exists.
I should like to say also that I agree wholly with the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) when he says that parliament should be kept fully informed of all developments in this field. I believe the hon. member made a suggestion that is worthy of consideration when he said that hon. members of parliament might be given the opportunity of going to Chalk River and of seeing what is being done there.
Committee on Atomic Energy
I have served on previous atomic energy committees, and speaking as one who has served on those committees and who has been at Chalk River several times, and who has had the opportunity of meeting the scientists who are working with reactors and in the various laboratories located there, I wish to say that I learned a great deal and I have developed an interest in this field which I might otherwise not have had although right from the day the first atomic scientists' bulletin was issued in the United States I have subscribed to these bulletins and have tried to follow the developments they have outlined as well as I could and the warnings they have given and the uses which they have indicated -can be made not only of one product, heat, but of the by-products to be used in medicine and in scientific fields generally.
I said that I had enjoyed the work of the previous committees and found the information useful. I should also like to say how much I was struck with the devotion as well as the ability of the scientists engaged at Chalk River. I was amazed to find how many of them were young. I have forgotten now just how many were under 30, but it was quite a number. I do remember that there was only a mere handful who were over 40 when we went up the first time, and I think when we went up the second time as well.
I was shocked last week to read that Dr. Cipriani had passed away. He was one of the foremost scientists in the world in this field and a more charming personality I have never met. In outlining the work of the atomic energy commission and that of his own particular field of medicine, not only did he give us the information which could be given but he did it in such a manner that we did not forget it. I just want to say that when we go there this time I know we shall miss Dr. Cipriani.
This committee will be dealing also with research. I am not sure that it was wise to put research and atomic energy before the one committee. It is a big field. We may be able to cover it, but having been on committees which have inquired into both atomic energy and research in the past I am of the opinion that two committees might have been advisable.
Now that atomic energy and atomic developments are under a crown company I think it is wise that we should go into the operations of that company. I have a great deal of sympathy for the idea that crown companies should be brought before parliamentary committees, annually if you will but at least periodically, in order that their operations

Committee on Atomic Energy may be examined into carefully by such committees. I think that that would be a step in the right direction. I know how difficult it is for members of parliament to attend to the business of the house and serve on committees. I do not think you could call every department and every crown company before a special committee to be examined every year, but I think it should be done periodically. We do examine two crown companies each year, Trans-Canada Air Lines Limited and Canadian National Railways, and from time to time we have the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation before a committee of parliament.
It is true that there is a tremendous interest in research. The establishment of the national research council years ago was something that has been of great benefit to our country. There is one criticism, however, I should like to make and that is that much of the result of the research which could be of guidance and indeed of some importance to the consuming public of this country is not made public.
In the United States they have the consumers' association. This began in a small way in one of the universities. They have a large population in the United States and consequently it was quite within the realm of possibility to set up an organization with sufficient funds to do a proper job for the consumer. That is what is being done by the consumers' research association in the United States. I often read the magazine they put out. I call it a magazine although they refer to it as a bulletin. I find therein a great deal of information regarding domestic supplies and other things which one might be inclined to buy from time to time. They make an appraisal of these different items.
I know that work of this description is being carried on to a limited extent by our national research council and the result of that research might be of great benefit to the people of this country who provide the funds for the research council. Those of us who were on the committee several years ago saw the results of investigations which had been made of a widely advertised detergent-I think I mentioned this before in the house-which while it may have washed clothes at the same time it would have destroyed them. Yet the people of this country had no information regarding those experiments carried out in the laboratories of the national research council.
I should like to see the people of Canada reap a direct benefit from research of this description carried on by the national research council. I am not indicating that that is the
[Mr. Coldwell.l
kind of research which the national research council does in any big way; I think it is more or less of a sideline with them. They have more important fields of research in which to operate. During the last few years we have provided the national research council with more laboratories situated on the Montreal road. I am sure we have all seen the impressive buildings in that area and I have no doubt that as time passes the facilities will be expanded and the national research council will be performing even greater services for our country and for industry than ever before.
I think that this committee will be one of our worthwhile committees and I am glad that my hon. friends have suggested that I be a member of the committee again this year. I am looking forward to participating in its work.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra suggested that the committee might go into military research, on the atomic side and, I believe, on the more general research side as well. I do not know how feasible that would be but I agree with his argument that there is possibly a waste of money which should be looked into and which might result in savings. I am convinced that the Department of National Defence should be examined into most closely by this house. We do not do it. I doubt if there are more than a few hon. members of the house who know what the expenditures of the department are, how they are made and to what extent they can be justified by those who make them.
I have every sympathy with any suggestion that is made for an investigation into the expenditures of the Department of National Defence provided it is made by parliament. I am not impressed with any arguments that it should be made by an outside body. I think the time has come when this house should go into those expenditures and therefore I have a great deal of sympathy with my hon. friend's suggestion with regard to military research.
I do not think I need to say anything more. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra covered a great deal of the ground which others might have been inclined to cover, and I am glad that he did. I think the time for appraisal of the work of the atomic energy authority and the national research council will be when the committee makes its report to the House of Commons. We shall then have authentic information before us and be able to speak more intelligently about what is going on in both fields.

subsubtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN NON-MILITARY RESEARCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we welcome the motion of the right

hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) for the appointment of a special committee to examine into the role of government in the field of military research in Canada, including operations in the field of atomic energy and the operations of the national research council. Not only is the importance of these matters increasing but the necessity of continued and accelerated research in every field of endeavour is in my opinion becoming increasingly more urgent as the days go by. Not only is research essential to the raising of the standards of living and the development of our economy but in many respects it would appear that research is necessary for our very survival itself.
I listened with interest to the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green). With respect to the atomic aspect of this motion, he stated that we as members of the House of Commons have very little information regarding the operations of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and developments in the field of atomic energy. As I listened to the hon. member I thought he had gleaned considerable information from different sources, and he certainly appeared to speak with some degree of authority on the various aspects of the situation. However, as he has said, I believe there is room for more information to be given to us with respect to the activities of these various corporations and the research that is carried on in connection with them.
With respect to the suggestion that there should be two committees rather than one, I believe it has considerable merit. As we think of the two fields that have been mentioned, it would certainly appear that one committee would not have the time to study and examine their operations fully. Therefore I think the suggestion that there should be two committees is a good one, and as it is a suggestion that has been advanced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) in times past I believe that possibly more consideration could be given to that matter.
The amendment that has been proposed will receive our support because we feel that in the setting up of a committee of this kind there should be avenues open to the members within their terms of reference whereby they can make a detailed study and examination of the entire situation. With regard to the first term of reference that is given for the guidance of the committee, namely, to examine into the role of government in the field of non-military research in Canada including operations in the field of atomic energy, we were of course ushered into the atomic era in 1945 when the impact of atomic power 67509-108J
Committee on Atomic Energy was first demonstrated in the bombing of the cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, Japan.
It seems to me a rather sad commentary on human intelligence that what has been called man's greatest achievement is the discovery and utilization of an energy that is capable of blasting man into oblivion. It seems to me that it was as a result of the fear and impetus provided by the prospect of world war that this energy was brought into being at the time that it was. We are living now in a day when this main deterrent to war must be converted to peaceful uses. Rather than being the destroyer of mankind it must be brought to a position where it becomes his servant and is developed in the interests of peace and for creative purposes. On page 8 of the ninth annual report of the atomic energy control board for 1954-55 we read the following:
During the past year there were developments of great significance in the power reactor program in Canada, notably the decision to design and construct a demonstration power reactor. This decision marked the turning point in the research and development effort which began in 1942. It is the first and an essential step in applying the nuclear information which has been accumulated in the post-war years.
Research in this field as far as possible uses of atomic energy are concerned is more or less in the preliminary stages and we believe that as research continues this tremendous energy and force will be utilized for the benefit of mankind and will take the place of many of the sources of power being utilized at the present time.
I do not propose to say any more about the first part of the motion dealing with atomic energy but I should like to refer to the second part which has to do with the operations of the national research council. I understand that the council has now been functioning for a considerable number of years and has been doing most commendable work in the various fields of investigation. The objectives of the national research council are very broad. They include the ascertaining and tabulation of various agencies in Canada which are carrying on scientific and industrial research, the noting and scheduling of lines of research and investigation that are being carried on, the co-ordinating of these agencies to prevent overlapping and the inducing of co-operation between these various agencies. One of its purposes is to acquaint itself with the problems of technical and scientific research and to apply that knowledge and skill to the solution of the various problems that confront industry. Its purpose as well is to make a scientific study of unused resources, waste and the by-products of farm, forests, fisheries and

Committee on Atomic Energy industries. It also has the purpose of enlarging the pool of scientific manpower available in these particular fields.
I have already stated that the council has done very commendable work, and I think we would do well to commend them today for the progress that has been made. On page 10 of the 38th annual report of the national research council of Canada for 1954-55 I find the following under the heading "General Statistics":
The national research council In 1954:
(i)	provided $2-5 millions to support fundamental research in the universities . . .
(ii)	employed 548 scientific staff, 711 technical personnel, 775 general service and administrative staff, and some 100 postdoctorate fellows;
(iii)	operated four laboratory divisions in the sciences; applied biology, pure chemistry, applied chemistry, pure and applied physics; operated three engineering divisions . . .
(iv)	answered technical inquiries from Canadian industries at the rate of 7,500 per year.
Certainly I think that shows a fine picture of the work that is being carried on. We commend the council for their activities and urge them to enlarge the scope of those activities, realizing the importance of their inquiries in all phases of research.
The resolution before us deals with the operations of the national research council. I suppose it takes in as well the various areas of research that are open to it. I realize, of course, that there are those avenues of research which are opened up through secondary industries, on the by-products of gas, oil and coal production. Included in the objectives of the research council we also find research in connection with our forest industries. Certainly this is an extremely wide field for research. Just to give an illustration of this particular field, I should like to refer to an article in the British Columbia Lumberman of February, 1956. It is entitled "Better Residue Use, Automation, Said Keys to Lumber Marketability". From this article I should like to read just a brief paragraph:
Mill residues can be used for hardboard and particle-board production, paper, and paperboard.
Then a little further on it continues as follows:
Several studies are under way to treat sawdust before its application to overcome the temporary nitrogen depletion induced by the sawdust. This treatment of sawdust would improve its characteristics as a soil conditioner.
This product is extremely important in the field of agriculture.
If pretreatment can be accomplished at a moderate cost, the potential market is vast.
I also had brought to my attention the research that is being carried on with respect to decadent cedar. This perhaps is of vital interest in the British Columbia economy because I am told that from a point just north

of Kamloops up as far as Prince George, and also in the Smithers and Terrace areas and along the coast there are billions of feet of decadent cedar. This constitutes a serious fire hazard and up until recently it has just been looked upon as something to be despised and something that caused a great many problems to the forest service. Research is being carried on into a pressed wood constructed of this decadent material. It has now been tested out. For instance, it was used in the steps of a bunkhouse in a lumber camp. Part of the step was constructed from fir, part from oak and part from decadent cedar pressed wood. After a period of use, with loggers treading on it with their great caulked boots, it was discovered that the fir had fairly well disintegrated, that the oak showed considerable wear but that little impression was made on this board that was made from decadent cedar. It would therefore appear that in this particular field of research alone vast fields are open. In this case I have cited, not only can they clean up the hazard that is caused by this condition but they can also place a valuable product upon the market. Others that have been mentioned in this particular reference to the research council included the fisheries. Possibly we can speak about that matter on the estimates at a later date. But all of these various fields open up tremendous avenues for research and for development. We feel that this is an extremely important aspect of our economy at the present time.
What about the role of government in these particular fields? I believe there is room for participation by various agencies. I think industry can play an important part in these research developments. Certainly it is doing that. A brief presented to the royal commission on forestry by the Canadian Pulp and Paper Association gives an illustration of what industry is prepared to do and is doing in the field of research. At page 29 of this brief we find the following:
Company research programs
All of the Integrated companies of the pulp and paper industry maintain research laboratories and full time crews engaged on various research programs and multiple investigations. In addition, all of these companies contribute considerable sums towards the various fundamental and applied research programs carried out by the Pulp and Paper Research Institute in Montreal. This organization is recognized as one of the world's leading institutions in the realm of cellulose research.
The total expenditure on this research by the above companies to improve technology, quality of product, processing and the practice of forestry, exceeds $850,000 annually. More than 90 research technicians are engaged full time in British Columbia on this work.
The above companies also contribute considerable sums from time to time to the British Columbia research council to aid in the work of various objective programs carried out by the council, as

well as a number of minor items of research and investigation outside the actual operations of the companies.
Industry is not prepared just to sit back and say that it is a government responsibility, that it is a field in which government should carry the load, but certainly is making a worth-while contribution in this field.
Our educational institutions are doing a remarkable work in this connection as well. Some of the provinces at least have set up research councils. I can speak for the province of British Columbia, as I know a little bit more about it than I do of the others. In that province the facilities have been greatly expanded and work is going on at an accelerated speed in the various fields of research in the forestry industry and in others. As I say, industry, our educational institutions and provincial governments are carrying on to the best of their ability. Personally I think that the federal government should accept considerable responsibility in this particular regard, encouraging all the agencies to intensify their studies to the end that our resources be utilized to their fullest possible extent. It would seem to me that they could assist from the technical point of view, the financial point of view and in many other ways as well. This afternoon we welcome the setting up of this committee and hope that its inquiries will stimulate interest in this vital work which is so essential in our modern age.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce

speechtext:
I do not wish to make a point of this. I just wish to point out that the resolution was put on the order paper early in the session last year and the motion was never brought forward for the consideration of the house. It has been put on the order paper this year and it is being considered today. I sincerely hope the motion

Committee on Atomic Energy will be approved and that the committee can undertake its work early in the session. If there is a complaint that it is unreasonable to expect one committee to investigate both branches of science, the committee could easily adjourn part of its work until next session, when it could be reconstituted and complete its work.
The reason the government has not provided for the calling of persons and papers is that this committee is carrying on its investigation in a field in which there are important secrets in the possession of those who would naturally appear before the committee. It has been said that much of the work at Chalk River has been declassified, and that is true. Canada has always taken the view that the work there should be declassified unless there is a very good reason for continuing secrecy. I think a witness to the fact that important secrets are in the possession of the staff at Chalk River is the security provisions that are observed at that place. We spend enormous amounts of money simply to protect the security of Chalk River. We have guards around the property. It is very difficult to get access to the property, except through Ottawa.
Why is secrecy preserved? The reason is that at Chalk River we do a considerable amount of work for the atomic energy commission of the United States having to do with the field of weapons. There is hardly any period when we have not had work of that kind in process at Chalk River. The reason is that the pile there is able to do some work which no other pile can carry out successfully. Then, too, we have almost free access to such information in the non-military field as is acquired by the atomic agency in the United States and also the atomic agency in the United Kingdom. The reason we had that complete access is that Canada has a wonderful record in the field of security. We have never had a serious breach of security from the Chalk River plant, and I think no other country can say as much about its own security.
I believe those who have served on similar committees in the past will know that both at Chalk River and in the research council any person will be produced, provided he is a senior man in the organization. So far as the production of papers is concerned, there are papers the secrecy of which must be guarded. It is much easier to let the senior personnel decide what papers can be produced without a breach of security, rather than to let the committee make that decision. If today this parliament decided that a committee would be appointed with authority to send for papers, I believe the flow of papers to

Atomic Energy of Canada Limited would be very sharply curtailed not later than tomorrow. Where there are secret documents in the possession of the organization, to authorize a committee to ask for those secret documents, with authority to demand that they be produced, would be fatal.
If there were any complaints that the right persons were not appearing before the committee, there would be a reason for the amendment before us today. If there were any suggestions that papers which could be properly produced before the committee were not being produced, then there would be a reason for this amendment. I claim that when there are papers that could not possibly be produced to the committee, and when there may be junior personnel in the both organizations unfamiliar with security regulations who might be asked for by the committee and allowed to talk freely in the fields which were their own particular responsibility, you would be creating a very dangerous situation indeed. That is the reason for the government's inability to agree to the amendment that is before us at the moment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are discussing the amendment, and the amendment would certainly put jt within the power of the committee to demand the production of classified information. For that reason the government must oppose it.
As far as the work of the committee is concerned, we are glad to have the committee go into every branch of atomic energy. We hope it will take an interest in Eldorado Mining and Refining. That is a fine operation and covers a broad field. We are very glad to have it explore the relations between Eldorado and the private uranium industry; we are glad to have the work of Northern Transportation explored.
I may say that each year since Northern Transportation has been in operation the rates on the Mackenzie have been reduced, and I rather expect there will be another reduction this year. The reason that has been possible is that the capital of the company has been expanded, the standard of equipment raised and improvements put in for traversing portages. It has been able to maintain a high standard of service and at the same time lower the costs of that service. The work of Northern Transportation Company has extended to the distant early warning line, and there again these might be classified material which cannot be produced; but I think almost any work of the Northern Transportation Company can be investigated by the committee without difficulty.
I would remind hon. members that the rates of Northern Transportation Company are approved by the board of transport commissioners. A hearing before the board of transport commissioners is necessary before there can be a revision of rates in that area.
I would also remind hon. members that there are competing services in the area which have a hard time getting along and each time there is a reduction in the rate by Northern Transportation there is a good deal of hardship caused amongst the competitors. However, the committee is free to weigh all 

those factors, and I would be very interested to see the report of the committee in that connection.
Mention was made of the fact that Canada at the moment does not produce uranium metal. Considerable progress has been made in that direction. We have had no great urge to get on with that phase of manufacturing, for the reason that we were able in the early stages to buy our metal from the United States at prices lower than we could possibly obtain by manufacturing the metal ourselves. That situation is changing, and I think within another 12 months Canada will be manufacturing its own metal.
