There is another organization meeting under the auspices of NATO in Europe which is also considering the problem. I assume these efforts will be joined in time and eventually we will get international rules which will provide the proper security. We hope so.
Mention was made of heavy water. The heavy water operation at Trail was one of the first established by the United States. Reference was made to the Montreal laboratory which was established in 1942 and disbanded in 1944. I think probably the small

quantities of heavy water which were used in that operation were obtained from Trail. That was one of the very early experimental operations, and I daresay at that time Trail may have been the only source of heavy water.
However, the process for making heavy water has been greatly improved and the cost of heavy water has been substantially lowered. The heavy water we bought for Chalk River was purchased from the atomic energy commission of the United States. It was delivered to Chalk River in trucks direct from south of the border. While I cannot guarantee that some of the heavy water did not come from Trail I would think it highly unlikely, from what I know of the transaction. However, I will be glad if the committee will look into that matter in its sessions this year and if I am wrong I shall be glad to be corrected.
I do not know that anything more needs to be said. The important matter before us today is whether or not the government motion shall be amended. As I say, we feel this particular amendment cannot possibly be accepted, and we trust that a vote can be held shortly.

subsubtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN NON-MILITARY RESEARCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like other hon. members who have preceded me in this debate I welcome the setting up of this particular committee. As a matter of fact the resolution itself has a rather familiar ring, because over the last three years, as Your Honour knows, I have had a resolution on the order paper to set up a committee to study ways and means of accelerating research in Canada.
Today there is naturally more interest in research than five years ago or even two years ago. We are in an atomic era, an age of automation, and our emergence into this period has been a long, slow process. The subject of research today is vital not only to this government and to governments on lower levels but to industry, labour and agriculture, and in fact it is of interest to every segment of our economy.
I was interested in what the minister's parliamentary assistant had to say respecting industry. I do not think any hon. member can stand up and say that it is the responsibility of government to do things that industry should do for itself. I do, however, maintain that crown companies, for instance, Polymer, which are under the jurisdiction of the government, could and should give leadership.
Speaking of research, they have given leadership. The report is available to anyone in this house or to anyone in Canada, wherein the president of Polymer said one or two 67509-109
Committee on Atomic Energy years ago that because of research the operations of the plant had been extremely successful. I was very glad to see that because for a number of years I, like everyone else, was conscious of the necessity of research. If we as a trading nation are going to maintain even the position we hold today it has to be done, I think, by more intensive research and by more money being spent in the field of research. While I did maintain in the past that we should take an occasional look at the tariff structure I have also maintained, as the minister himself said a year ago in discussing this matter, that in many instances industry could cut out frills and reduce costs.
On that very subject, according to authorities which I have read, our country is in the same position as the United States was in 1920 with respect to research. That to me is most lamentable. True enough many of our industries here are branches of industries in the United States or in some other foreign country and have depended too much in the past on the research done in those particular countries. I think we will all agree with that. I should like to point out, however, that industries in this country should become more research conscious. It is true that some of the large industries have constructed laboratories and have hired scientists and technicians but the strange thing to me, and I think all hon. members will find it strange, is that very few of the top scientists in this country are working in industry.
I do not mind making a startling statement when I say, .as I suggested a moment ago, that many of our top industries are simply branches operating in Canada, such as the chemical industry and I might mention particularly the oil industry; we know Imperial Oil Limited is a subsidiary of Standard Oil of New Jersey. In recent years they have been spending a great deal more on research than in the past, but they were dependent on the research carried on by the parent company. Here we have a large organization which is not spending in proportion to what another Standard subsidiary is spending, and I refer to Humble Oil Company. I think the statement was made the other day by its president, Mr. Jack White, that they were spending many millions of dollars this year on research. That was an encouraging statement. They are enlarging the laboratory at Sarnia, and will now be more independent of the parent company.
But other oil companies do not have their laboratories in this country. I can think of one company with its refinery not too far from the city hall in Sarnia which depends for its research work upon engineers in New

Committee on Atomic Energy York. There are other established oil companies in this country which also have their research done by the parent companies. They make no attempt to hire engineers and graduates from our own universities in order to establish research branches which are so important to the success of any company.
Industry in this country must realize that the time has passed when they can depend upon their parent companies for research. If we are going to maintain our position as a trading nation we must take advantage of the knowledge of these engineers and scientists. The companies that do take advantage of this knowledge are the ones that will be successful. I could quote the statements of different companies.
What is alarming to me and I think to every hon. member of the house is that we do not seem to have a co-ordinated research plan in this country like they have in Great Britain. There they have a scientific committee and if I mentioned that one thing without saying anything else this afternoon I think I would be doing a lot to impress my fellow members in this house with the importance of this subject. They have had this committee for years. It sits in the house in London and is composed of members of parliament with a member from each scientific society or association. They have about 175 to 190 members who meet regularly. The chairman is a senior member of the government.
No change was made in this practice even during the time the Labour party was in power. The committee advises all departments of the government on matters with which research is connected. I should like to refer briefly to "This is Britain" a monthly news letter issued by the United Kingdom information office in Ottawa. This particular issue is dated May, 1954, and I quote:
The parliamentary scientific committee, which has been described by Lord Samuel as "unique in its history and, indeed, unique among the parliaments of the world", recently published its annual report for 1953.
The committee is referred to as one of a number of informal, unofficial, all-party groups which have grown up spontaneously but which had managed to establish itself with more continuity and formality than some of the others. It goes on:
Membership is open to members of parliament of any party in both the House of Lords and the House of Commons, and also to the nominated representatives of those scientific and technological organizations in the country which, under its constitution, can be affiliated. No organization can be a member of it which is engaged in promoting some scientific process or project for profit or commercial gain.
iMr. Murphy (Lambton West).]

It states further:
Membership in 1953 comprised 163 members of parliament and representatives of 85 scientific and technological institutions.
The aims and activities are said to be:
1.	Provide members of parliament with authoritative scientific information from time to time in connection with debates.
2.	Bring to the attention of M.P.'s and government departments the results of scientific research and technical development which bear upon questions of current public interest.
3.	Arrange for suitable action through parliamentary channels whenever necessary to insure that proper regard is had for the scientific point of view.
4.	Examine all legislation likely to affect the above and take such action as may be suitable.
That is amazing in view of what has taken place in the thinking of many people in this country and in Great Britain with respect to research. I have here a report of one of the Haldane lectures by Sir Henry Tizard dealing with research. This was delivered on May 5 of last year, and the lecturer drew upon his own wide fund of experience in order to discuss some of the problems which exist. He went on to discuss the problems which arise from the intellectual gap between the man trained in science and the man trained in the humanities, and advocated that the majority of future administrators should have a broad scientific education.
I think many will agree that it would be preferable in this atomic age and age of automation if more members of the government were scientifically trained. I am not criticizing the government because of its present set-up, because we who were members of previous atomic energy committees know that never at any time was there any conscious spirit of politics in any of our discussions. The committee members have had a high regard for each other, and I hope that spirit will be maintained. An astounding thing about research in this world is indicated in this lecture, where it states:
Fifty years ago there was very little conscious effort to enlist the help of science in problems of defence.
In other words, 50 years ago there was very little interest in science or in research. The lecturer went on to say:
Mr. Harold Cox, a Cambridge mathematician and economist, probably presented a very general view when, after referring to French and German developments, he said: "We shall be far more strengthening our national position by buying the best that foreign inventiveness can give than by making wasteful experiments at our own expense".
The attitude in that regard has changed. In another lecture on the strategy of research delivered on January 12, 1956, we find the following:
During the past 50 years research has changed from luxury into necessity of existence.

I think it is about time that industry in Canada took upon itself the responsibility of having its research work done in Canada and not by the parent companies regardless of where they may be situated. This scientific committee in Great Britain has been referred to by the leaders of government for the past several years as a body which was mainly responsible for Great Britain being able to get out of the difficult position in which it was after the war and again become a great trading nation. That was not only the opinion of members of the house and of the different governments in Great Britain; it was also the opinion of casual observers outside of Great Britain.
I should like to emphasize that because, after all is said and done, what these experts can say on the subject is much more important to us than what I can contribute. I have a report here from the United States department of commerce dated February, 1952. It is headed, "The Rising Inventive Competition of Great Britain, A Challenge to U.S. Development Engineers and Manufacturers." In the report they have this to say:
One of the principal instrumentalities in improving their industrial and scientific economic position is their parliamentary and scientific committee, which in itself is an unofficial partnership of members of the houses of lords and of commons on the one hand and members of the national scientific and engineering institutions and of recognized research organizations and bodies on the other.
I am naturally interested, Mr. Speaker, in the amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra which I seconded, because in my former resolutions I have always asked for witnesses to be called. I do think that if the committee were empowered to call outside witnesses, witnesses other than those in the employ of crown companies, we would get the benefit of their advice, and in my opinion it is vitally important that we should have it.
On the matter of the scientific committee in Great Britain, I recall that a couple of years ago Sir Robert Watson-Watt spoke to a club in Ottawa. He is certainly well known to all members of the government, because he was an adviser to the defence board during the war. At that time he pointed out how important it was to have a scientific committee such as they have in Britain, where complacency has no place.
In the past I have quoted many authorities. I am on record over several years. In fact I am on record to such an extent that one individual, writing in the January issue of a magazine called Canadian Chemical Processing Outlook, incorporated a good deal of what I had said and made several suggestions which have been made by me in the house on 67509-109J
Committee on Atomic Energy more than one occasion. I should like to take this opportunity to correct one thing he said. He stated that all members of all the different parties in the house had agreed to a scientific committee. As a matter of fact the matter was never discussed to that extent, and I believe I am the only member in the house who ever suggested it. To that extent, at any rate, he is wrong.
I have said before that we would like to have such witnesses appear before the committee, and I hope that during the dinner hour or later the minister will change his opinion; because if we were able to call such witnesses it would provide the medium for a combined approach, political, educational, industrial and agricultural, to the question of research in Canada and what parliament could or should do to accelerate efforts in this field.
When the minister spoke a few minutes ago he said that one reason we should not call witnesses or send for papers or records was that all the wisdom of several countries is, according to him, on file at Chalk River. I do not know whether or not that is accurate. I have always had the idea that the McCarran act, introduced in the United States because of espionage here during and after the war, was used as the excuse for that nation not to pass on any information to Great Britain and Canada. Whether that legislation is still in effect I do not know, but if it is I wonder whether the minister made his statement more or less off the cuff and it is not actually correct.
As I said earlier, if we have the power to call witnesses we would like to call those I mentioned a while ago. We would like to call those engaged in agricultural and scientific research and the presidents of universities, because our universities are in a desperate situation today. They are called upon to face many problems and their presidents could give us ideas that I think would be important to the members of the committee. In addition, we could hear representatives of agriculture, labour and industry whose contributions I believe would be valuable to the committee.
I say this because, after all is said and done, no civil servant is going to come before any committee and say anything that is contrary to government policy. We would not expect him to do so. But the independent witness is free to come here and give evidence from his own experience that I think would be valuable. As another reason for not calling such witnesses the minister said something about them going to Chalk River. It was never our intention at any

Committee on Atomic Energy time that these witnesses would go to Chalk River or would see anything of a classified nature in the form of either documents or machinery. While I am sure the committee will serve a most useful purpose, I am satisfied it would be much more effective if we could hear such witnesses.
I should like for a moment to reply to a statement made by the parliamentary assistant in introducing the resolution. He mentioned that Canada spent $70 million last year on research. That is only about $4.50 per capita. I have gone on record before, and the statement has never been challenged, that in the fiscal year 1954-55 the United Kingdom spent $15 per capita and the United States $25 per capita. In the same year the central governments of those countries, the United Kingdom and the United States, spent $11 and $15 per capita respectively. These amounts are far in excess of the per capita spending in this country.
We also have in Canada a problem that has been discussed for ten or eleven days, the disposal of agricultural surpluses. I am one of those who believe that politics will never solve the farm surplus problem. I also believe that if we made better use of our scientific knowledge agriculture probably would not be in the position it is in today. It is a rather strange thing that Holland and Denmark, where agriculture enjoys the highest reputations as a profession, do not have any problem in disposing of their agricultural products. They have adopted scientific methods. In other words, they have successfully adapted industrial methods to farming. There is no such thing as a subsidy for agricultural products in either of those countries.
Of course in this country we find that we have terrific surpluses of agricultural products that are hard to dispose of. I might mention here that two or three years ago the chemurgic industries in the United States acquired and disposed of about $1J billion worth of surplus farm products which were hard to dispose of, and in fact a good part of them would have become waste if those industries had not acquired them. I think the same thing could be done here if our research were co-ordinated, which it would be if we had the scientific planning to which I referred a while ago.
We have research done by the provinces, by various departments of the federal government and in various universities. But there does not seem to be any planning to get the best out of the research, and to get the most out of the money spent on research.

I believe we must bear in mind that the universities today are facing some difficulty, as I said a while ago.
Something which is important to us in this country is the upsurge of engineering education in Russia. They have already surpassed the western world in the number of engineers they have graduated. It might be easy enough to say yes, they graduate 50 per cent more engineers than do the United States, Britain and Canada, and that would not mean very much because it might be possible that those engineers were not properly trained. But as a matter of fact, we now know that those engineers they graduate in Russia are top trained men. As a matter of fact they were a revelation to our own scientists and to those of the western world who met at Geneva some time last year. We might as well face the problem here, namely that we must give more attention to education in this country.
I think the only way in which we are going to get more students in the universities to take up engineering is to initiate our work in the collegiates, through our teachers and boards, and see that these scholarly students in the higher grades are given an opportunity or are induced, really, to take up engineering as their life work. When they get to university we should probably adopt the same system as they have in Britain, with bursaries. In any event these smart, intelligent students should be encouraged to take up engineering, mathematics and physics in order that they can make in this country the contribution we need from our own people. We must not let these people, after they graduate, go to the United States or any other country. That trend has been going on for far too long. Years ago I said that, in the case of these engineers, the crown companies should give leadership in hiring them and also in the payment of their salaries.
Just the other day, Mr. Speaker, we regretted very much to see in the press a report that 40 or 50 of these young Canadian graduates in engineering left one of our Toronto area airplane factories to join a similar industry in California at a 100 per cent increase in salary. In order to see the demand there is for engineers in that country all you need to do is pick up the Sunday New York Times. This country in the past has faced and is going to continue to face the emigration to the United States of our top scientists and graduates in engineering and physics because they are going to pay them 50 to 100 per cent more than we are paying at this time. If we are going to keep them, we must pay them more money.

I will say this. There are in Canada many scientists-we see them at Chalk River-to whom the salary or remuneration is not one of the considerations for staying in Canada. The man to whom the leader of the C.C.F. referred this afternoon is one of them. He was so devoted to his work that it did not make any difference to him whether he had $50 a day or $10 a day. He drove an old 1929 Ford car to go fishing and he was happy in his work.
But the engineers who graduate are not all of that kind. These young people will have families to support, in all probability, after a few years. We must keep them in Canada. We are going to need them. Industry must take the responsibility of hiring these people to do research in this country.
To the crown companies of this country I say, give leadership to the other industries in this country and pay the salaries to which these people are entitled, and thus prevent them from going to the United States or some other country. It has cost the taxpayers of this country no less than $25,000 to educate each of these young men. Let us keep them here. They are an asset to this country. We want them. As this country develops, with all our wealth of natural resources which no other country in the world possesses- they are hardly scratched-these men are as necessary to us as are the minerals that are in those underground deposits.
If it is necessary for this government to make grants for education, let it take the responsibility that is necessary in order to maintain our economic position in the world today. Let the government make these grants. We must have engineers. Somebody might hesitate to take the grants. There is no reason why in some way or other moneys could not be made available to these students. I will say this. Because of the high taxation in this country the revenues of many universities have been drying up. I suggest that donations, up to a reasonable amount, made to universities by people or companies be exempt from income tax. I hope that more will be granted in the future than has been granted in the last few years in order that we may meet the challenge which this country faces.
I am going to say this, Mr. Speaker. This subject reminds me, as I think it does most people, of what the Red Queen said to Alice:
... it takes all the running you can do, to keep in the same place. If you want to get somewhere else, you must run at least twice as fast.
On reading that statement first, as I recall it, I thought there was not much to it. But I think anyone interested in this particular subject will read it a second time.
Committee on Atomic Energy
For three or four minutes of the time at my disposal, Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with a problem which we faced last fall, in spite of what the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra said about my dealing with research. I may say that I am going home tonight so I will not be obliged to face his comments. I will not say any more about the matter.
Last fall, Mr. Speaker, I think Canadians not only in Ontario but all across this country were alarmed by the statement made by Mr. R. L. Hearn, the Ontario hydro chairman. I think it was made some time in September or October. He warned the Canadian government, and I know this appeared in the press of Ontario, to broaden its atoms for peace program or miss the boat. To me the statement was most important because, as you know, the Ontario hydro, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and a certain electrical company-the three of them-are participating in the construction of a plant to produce electricity from nuclear power. He suggested that more industry and utilities participate, and that the shutters of secrecy surrounding most of this country's atomic research should be removed. He went on to say that with the completion of the St. Lawrence hydro project and the additional power from the 50,000 cubic feet per second now being developed above Niagara Falls, Ontario will have used up all its hydro potential.
In Ontario we do not have oil or gas to any extent. Down in my area we have some, but it is not a big factor when compared with the total consumption. In this province we have a great deal of uranium. We do not know-and maybe we shall not know for a century-how much uranium there is in the province of Ontario, let alone in the other provinces of Canada. This resource should be developed. I foresee the time, probably in about 15 years, when we will be able to develop hydro power from atomic energy more cheaply than we are getting it today from water resources.
The president of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, I think it was sometime in November, said in New York that Canada is considering an exchange of information on the peaceful uses of atomic energy with a number of countries besides the United States and Great Britain. In my opinion the irony of that is that here we were willing to exchange information with the United States and Britain, yet the United States would not give us any information, or very little. As I understand it, she would not even give Great Britain any information regarding how the Nautilus was powered by atomic energy, when some people from Great Britain were in the United

Committee on Atomic Energy States last fall. The president of Atomic Energy says he is going to make this information available to other countries. I assume that is quite all right.
It is unfortunate that the western democracies do not share the information they have on atomic energy and other aspects of this atomic era. It simply means that if the United States is ahead of Britain in one development and will not release the information, Britain will probably get it within a year or two, because there is no such thing as keeping such information very long. The scientists in one country are as good as in another, and they will get the information sooner or later. We all know of instances in which scientists in different countries have come up with the same idea at different times.
It was profoundly disquieting to read that our Soviet rivals had already passed the western world in the industrial application of atomic energy. More important, it is increasingly evident that the Soviet union intends to use the industrial atom as an instrument of foreign policy, along with and perhaps in preference to the military atom. Nations which are poor in natural resources, whose resources are poorly distributed and which are now emotionally and politically unstable, could become our industrial equals and unfriendly competitors through the use of atomic power reactors donated by Soviet Russia. The only way out of the world's political and economic dilemma is to provide the power for agrarian nations to become industrialized, and for partly industrialized nations to industrialize completely.
I think we must now face up to the fact that in the atomic age dollars are no longer power. The prime material power is the absolute power of atomic energy. With the atom, mankind has finally secured a key to power unlimited, and power is the prime mover of industrialization. We must use industrial atomic energy to increase the living standards of the so-called have-not nations. As a back bencher I express the hope, for what it is worth, and I think the hope is shared by many members of this house, that the western democracies today, as they face the challenge of the U.S.S.R. and her satellites, can work together as a team and pool such information as we have been discussing in order to be collectively in a better position to challenge any forces that might be interested in overpowering us.
We have today a resurgence of industry through atomic energy. There is a great deal of interest in different countries in atomic energy today where even a few years ago there was not. As an illustration, France has
IMr. Murphy (Lambton West).]
a department of government to deal with research. As a matter of fact, this year Italy has spent more money on research than any other European country. These smaller countries, Mr. Speaker, like Norway and Denmark, and some of those in western Europe, are spending a great deal more per capita on research than we are. Strange as it may seem, they appear to have recovered economically and are today in a competitive position. If we in this country are to meet foreign competition in foreign markets and in our own markets, we must do so through research.
I am going to say that nature, history and geography have combined to richly endow this country, but prosperity and employment are not ensured simply because those resources lie within our boundaries. They will be ensured only to the extent that we as a people utilize those resources. As I said a moment ago, and I think it is worth emphasizing, today we should be in a position where we process more of these resources instead of buying back the finished products after manufacture in foreign countries.
The papers are filled with articles these days by scientists and industrial leaders speaking of the need for accelerated research and the dangers of our continued dependence on other countries. We knew last year, Mr. Speaker, that Britain, which is foremost in the field of research, had no unemployment. The same situation prevailed in the United States, whereas in this country we had a goodly number. I will not mention the number because I do not want it even suggested I am making political capital out of this sacred subject.

I shall recognize the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) in just a moment. First I should like to presume to make a suggestion for the consideration of the house. subsubtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN NON-MILITARY RESEARCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think what I have to say will come within the ambit of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, and support his contention as to the necessity of the committee having power to call before it certain witnesses, witnesses who would not necessarily be available however willing the government might be to provide them from among their own employees. I believe that in considering this question, Mr. Speaker, we have to face the fact that today science has become so specialized that very often the opinions of eminent figures in
Committee on Atomic Energy one branch of science are of little value in considering another aspect of the same question.
The matter I want to discuss this afternoon is one that I have raised before in the house on other occasions, namely the possible genetic effects of our activities in the atomic field. In order to place before the house the serious view that is taken by many eminent scientists with regard to the possibilities of the atomic age, I want to quote from an article by Dr. A. H. Sturtevant, of the California Institute of Technology, who is generally regarded as one of the leading geneticists of the United States. He had this to say on the danger of mutations from high-energy irradiation. He sets forth the facts in this form:
1.	High-energy irradiation produces mutations.
2.	The frequency of induced mutations is directly proportional to the dosage of irradiation. There is almost certainly no threshold value below which irradiation is ineffective.
He cites numerous other basic facts with regard to that, and later on he has this to say:
The "maximum permissible" exposure will become a matter for careful consideration If nuclear reactors come to be widely used as power sources, since under those conditions also there will be an increase in the background radiation. The amount and character of such increases will depend in part on the type of reactors used, and on the details of their design and operation-and it is a matter of public concern that this factor, as well as economic ones, be taken into account in a program for the non-military development of atomic energy.
I suggest this to the house, Mr. Speaker, that a committee that has not the power to call before it competent geneticists as distinguished from physicists to give their opinions to the committee on the possible dangers of an atomic energy program is a committee that is not going to be able to ask the questions that we should be asking very definitely today.
I listened carefully to the minister's reasons for refusing to accept the amendment of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, and I wondered just how it is going to be possible for this committee to do what the resolution suggests it ought to do, namely examine into the non-military operations in the field of atomic energy, if that committee is not going to be able to call before it competent witnesses to give it some idea of the possible results of whatever program may be revealed to us during the sittings of that committee.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, I wondered whether the minister's objections to this amendment were not perhaps based on his reluctance to assume the difficult job of riding herd on the government majority on that committee; because of course it is perfectly obvious that if the government members on the committee

Committee on Atomic Energy are on their toes then no witnesses, no papers and no records will be asked for that would in any way embarrass the government or endanger the secrecy of classified information. But I do seriously suggest, sir, that we are not going to obtain an effective picture of our atomic energy program unless we have some idea of the possible dangers of that program for peaceful purposes.
I hold in my hand an extract from the Canadian Chemical Processing magazine of April of last year which contains an article by Professor James G. Foulkes, M.D., of the University of British Columbia, on the question of the dangers of background irradiation. In this article Dr. Foulkes quotes Dr. H. J. Muller of the United States, another leading United States geneticist, a gentleman who you will recall, Mr. Speaker, was refused permission by the atomic energy commission of the United States to appear before the recent Geneva conference on atomic energy. It was generally supposed at that time that Dr. Muller's evidence as a geneticist would be embarrassing to the United States defence authorities.
Dr. Muller is quoted in this article as saying:
Despite a number of unfortunate publicized statements by non-geneticists casting doubt on the mutagenic effectiveness of small doses of radiation, the work has gone so far as to make it inconceivable, on physico-chemical grounds, for a single ionization track traversing a cell nucleus to be without its proportionate probability of inducing a gene mutation.
He goes on to say:
Such considerations have led one scientist to conclude that "the long-range genetic danger of exposure of mankind as a whole to low-level, but widespread and persistent radioactivity, is the most ominous of all the dangers of the atomic age."
I have read the reports published by our government on this matter, reports published by the atomic energy control board of Canada, by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and by Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited, but I have not found the slightest reference in any of them to any investigations or research in this matter. Apparently we are prepared to go ahead blindly, not to consider the possible genetic results, and hope that the economic benefits may blind us to any possible dangers to the human species. I think, Mr. Speaker, this is a question on which we have to ask some very serious questions, and this committee is not going to be able to ask them if the Minister of Trade and Commerce persists in refusing to allow it to call competent witnesses to give us advice on this matter.
A few weeks ago I had the opportunity to get in contact indirectly with one of the


leading geneticists of Great Britain, Professor J. B. S. Haldane. A member of my family is studying biochemistry and genetics under Professor Haldane. In discussing the danger of genetic mutation from both military and non-military uses of atomic energy, Professor Haldane asserted that while he could consider it was not yet probable that the increase in background irradiation was sufficient to cause dangerous mutations, he was very insistent on this point that no one knows. And because no one knows, Professor Haldane has instigated an inquiry and an investigation at the British atomic energy centre at Harwell into the mutation effects on various laboratory animals of exposure to radiation at the level that we can expect with the widespread use of atomic reactors. I would feel much happier in my own mind, Mr. Speaker, if I could see some evidence in Canada of a similar anxiety and care to insure the future of the human species. It may sound laughable, but I say this. There is no one in this chamber, not a single soul, whose opinion is of any value.

subsubtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN NON-MILITARY RESEARCH
speechtext: And not many outside of it, either.

subsubtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN NON-MILITARY RESEARCH
speechtext:
There are a few outside, but hon. members of the government and of this house persistently close their ears to the warnings of the few people in the world who know.
I suggest, sir, that such a course can only lead to catastrophe. I would hope that whether or not the government decides that it is going to permit a committee of this house to investigate these activities and call before it competent witnesses, we shall have before long some statement from the government which will indicate that it realizes that the development of atomic power is fraught with very great danger and its operations must be conducted with the utmost care.
I have heard, for instance, no indication from the government nor have I seen in any publication in this country an indication that the serious and difficult problem of the disposal of atom waste has been in any way effectively coped with. It is a problem to which the scientists of Great Britain are giving a great deal of attention at the present moment, and it is a cause of great anxiety to them. We in this country appear to be quite blandly indifferent to the possible problems we are creating. I suggest that while we may revel in the idea of endless power produced for a minimum of expense we should also realize there is only one purpose in producing power in any way at all, and that is to add to the happiness and satisfaction of human beings. But we are not going

to do that if we permit in succeeding generations more and more deleterious mutation. Scientists tell us that the probabilities are that they are nearly all degenerative in nature and cumulative in their effects.
1 should like to see this committee set up, and I should like to see this committee have some inclination to reassure us on this point, because this happens to be one of the things which once done can never be undone. Once we have succeeded in creating a level of background irradiation that does carry with it this danger, there is nothing on earth that we can do to reduce that level in the future. It is there for good, or for evil in this case.
I hope the Minister of Trade and Commerce will realize that the people of Canada through the hon. members of this house are entitled to the utmost frankness in the way of disclosures of information about the program that has been undertaken by the government. I hope if he is not going to do that he will then alter this resolution so this committee will not be described as one which is to examine into the operations of the government, because obviously it is not going to be allowed to do this; but it will be described instead as a committee of this house to receive certain information from the government with regard to its atomic energy program.

speechtext:
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. I greatly welcome this committee to inquire into the fields of atomic energy and the national research council. I think the committee will do extremely useful work in
Committee on Atomic Energy disseminating information to the general public about such bodies as the national research council that the public at the present time does not have the advantage of learning.
I think at the moment we should realize why we are faced with the necessity of setting up such a committee. The reason for that, I believe, is quite apparent. The reason is the growth of the uranium industry in Canada during the last three or four years. We might ask, too, why we have had such a growth and how we have developed a uranium industry in such a short period of time. I think it is entirely due to the foresight and optimism of our Minister of Trade and Commerce. We owe a great deal to the minister in this as we do in many other respects.
Because of his foresight I am in a position to say to you now that in my riding we are presently producing about three-quarters of the uranium produced in Canada. This has come about within the last three years, and is entirely the brain child of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In that regard as in many other matters in which his foresight is apparent in this country, I think he has contributed more to the standard of living of the Canadian people than any other man either living or dead.
I should like to join with those hon. members who a few minutes ago observed that they hoped this committee would be able to look into the operation at Chalk River as has been done before, and also that it might look into the production end of uranium in the Beaverlodge uranium area. I do hope the committee will be able to do this because tremendous strides in production have been made in that area in the last two or three years, and I think it should be looked into.
As I mentioned a moment ago, I think the people of this country are poorly informed concerning what bodies such as the national research council do. This was forcibly brought to my attention last fall when the new mill at the Gunnar uranium mine at Beaverlodge was opened. The Gunnar mine is unique among uranium mines. There is nothing like it in the world and very likely there will not be another mine like it. It is the only open pit uranium mine in existence. As such it is a potentially low-cost operation.
To give hon. members some idea of how it works out, may I say that a charge of 300 pounds of dynamite produces about 15,000 tons of ore. The ore is picked up by 3-yard shovels and dumped into 30-ton Euclid trucks, which then make a quarter mile run to the ball mill. This plant was designed on a test tube basis by a gentleman named Ross in the national research council.

Committee on Atomic Energy
I want to give hon. members some idea of what research can do for industry. Mr. Ross asked that 100 tons of ore from the mine be sent to Ottawa for processing. After a year's research he found that there were four processes which could be made applicable to the ore, and he picked out the acid leach process for the Gunnar mill. He designed the equipment from the test tube investigations and mining men who were present at the opening, such as Jules Timmins and others who had spent their lives in mining, said that it was the first time that they had seen a mill anywhere approach its rated capacity within less than a year or perhaps two years. In this particular instance the mill reached 125 per cent of its capacity within two weeks, something that has never occurred in mining in any place in the world.
That was due entirely to the research done by this Mr. Ross at the national research council in Ottawa. The net result is that you have an operation there that can compare most favourably with operations in other parts of the world. Other operations lose from 5 to 10 per cent of uranium, but this process was 99J per cent perfect as far as recovery of uranium from the ore is concerned. It is even better now, and I understand at the present time they get 99 f per cent recovery.
It will be seen from this what research can contribute to our economy. This mill was designed for 1,250 tons a day, but within two weeks of its opening was handling 1,500 tons of ore a day. This is a different type of operation from the Federal mill at Beaver-lodge, only 20 miles north. There they are mining in a conventional manner. They process about 650 tons of ore a day, and it takes nearly twice as many men to do the job as at Gunnar.
When I go into this district I am always asked when the Minister of Trade and Commerce is going to go in there to look at what they consider he is responsible for. They are quite ready to admit that that place would not exist if it had not been for the foresight of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I hope that when this committee goes to work it will be given an opportunity to go in and look at the mills up there.
I can tell hon. members that at Gunnar they will find a perfect example of automation. There are four chemical processes which are of a split second change nature. The changes from one to the other are all done automatically from a panel. No one is required for the operation of the plant. If there is a breakdown in any part of the process that is indicated on the panel, which also indicates where the trouble is and what


has to be done to fix it. Practically all the men are employed in actually getting out the ore and keeping in repair the machines used for drilling and so on. There are two or three supervisors walking around the plant, but they are all you will see.
If this committee goes anywhere I hope it will visit the Beaverlodge area where it can see the Eldorado mill. The Gunnar mill is to be expanded from 1,250 tons to 2,500 tons. The Lorado mill is to be constructed this year with a capacity of some 1,500 tons. This expansion will place Canada in 12 months' time at the very top of the world's uranium producers. If the committee does go there I hope the Minister of Trade and Commerce will go along so that the people up there will be able to congratulate him upon his outstanding foresight, imagination and, something for which he is often criticized, his optimism.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
