subsubtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN NON-MILITARY RESEARCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take part briefly in the discussion tonight because I feel that we are dealing with one of the most important subjects that could come before the House of Commons. In my opinion the subject of research, as we move into the age of automation, is going to be increasingly important as we attempt to grapple with the industrial changes that will arise and, more important than the industrial implications, the sociological effects that will follow in the wake of the increasing trend toward automation.
In my remarks tonight I am going to concentrate, as has already been emphasized, on

the amendment before the house. The slight modification in form that has just been presented by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra makes the task somewhat easier, because it seems to remove the one objection that has been forthcoming from the government side up to the present time concerning an amendment of this kind. I feel it is very important that the committee have the privilege of calling for persons and papers; otherwise the basic purpose of the committee is going to be thwarted.
By very definition the subject of research requires the broadest treatment and access to every available source of information. Because of that it is important that there be no artificial restrictions imposed. As has been pointed out by previous speakers, the resolution as it stands on the order paper is somewhat restricted in nature, in that it confines the discussion to the fields of atomic energy and the operations of the national research council.
I listened carefully to the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey) in his introductory statement, and I noticed that there was some hope for a broadening of the terms of reference when he added to the two main categories an additional broad category in words to this effect, that the committee would consider research in all its general aspects. If his 'interpretation of the phrase, "consider research in all its general aspects", is similar to mine, then I feel we have a fairly broad approach to the problem of research available to the committee.
I had intended to concentrate on one aspect of the problem, but just before the house rose at six o'clock the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) introduced a discussion of the probable genetic effects of atomic radiation on human beings. As he indicated, this has been one of the burning issues that have arisen in popular discussion since the advent of the atomic age. The hon. member for Nanaimo suggested that there had not been much formal action taken by way of consideration of the effects on human heredity of atomic radiation.
I should like to add one small piece of information to that which he has already placed before the house. Last fall the subject of the peaceful uses of atomic energy received somewhat prolonged consideration at the general assembly of the United Nations. One of the recurring topics under that general heading that appeared in the committee discussions there was the probable dangers to human heredity from the increasing level of atomic radiation. At the present time some 20 nations are meeting in the United States in an
Committee on Atomic Energy attempt to set up an atomic energy commission which will have as one of its major considerations the gathering and the sharing of information on all aspects of the peaceful uses of atomic energy. This, of course, would include all available information concerning the probable effects on human mutation.
I use the word "probable" advisedly, because actually very little scientific research has taken place concerning this problem. There have been plenty of armchair scientists who have indulged in speculation concerning the facts, but there is very little concrete scientific data. The phrase "armchair scientists" was used, incidentally, by the late Dr. Cipriani, who was Canada's expert on this matter at the last general assembly session of the United Nations, and I join with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold well) in regretting sincerely the sudden passing of that eminent physicist.
Dr. Cipriani, who had given some consideration to the problem of the genetic effects of atomic radiation, had come to the conclusion as a result of his investigations that there was no immediate danger. He quoted by way of example some rather interesting experiments that had been taking place in Sweden. Sweden has done some initial experimental work in this regard because it is a small country, and there they can control the data with which they are working. To a large extent the population is homogeneous and occupies a small geographic area. One further factor of importance is that the level of radiation is considerably higher in Sweden than in most other areas.
Some very worth-while work is being done on the effects of atomic radiation on human heredity, and I am sure that when the atomic energy commission arranged by the United Nations Organization at its last general assembly session is functioning adequately, this problem will be coped with successfully. I merely add those words in passing.
I now come to the main subject with which I wish to deal tonight. Of course I support the position taken by the other spokesmen of this party, namely the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra, and the hon. member for Lambton West, who from time to time in this house has taken the lead in urging action on the general problem of stimulating research activity in this country. I should like to come back to the aspect that I have stressed cn two previous occasions in this house when there has been an opportunity to discuss the general subject of research. I refer to the role of government-to use the phrase that is included in the general resolution-in social science research.
1724	HOUSE OF
Committee on Atomic Energy
The resolution stresses non-military research in Canada. From the use of that phrase I take it that the government, in putting forward this resolution, is trying to get away from the emphasis that has dominated research activity in this country ever since the founding of the national research council in 1917. It grew out of the emergency of world war I. Since that time the major emphasis in research in Canada has been on the military aspects, the development of weapons or, as that particular type of development is popularly known, the hardware aspects of research.
In Canada a small beginning has been made in the realm of social science research on the part of the government as well as on the part of voluntary organizations. We have in Canada a social science research council which is largely a voluntary group, and we also have a humanities research council. They have been doing notable pioneering work in the important area of social science research. The government also is operating in this field to a certain extent. For example, the national research council includes one psychologist in an advisory capacity, so that at least the door is slightly ajar for the entrance of social science research activity. The defence research board has moved a little bit further into the area because it is employing psychologists to deal with some of the general problems of human relations that arise when you have men concentrated together in the various branches of the armed forces.
Perhaps the most worth-while contribution in the field of human relations, however, has been in the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, where we find sociologists and social psychologists doing some excellent work in the problem of the integration and assimilation of our new citizens. That is an extremely important task to which this particular department has devoted some attention. Then of course you have any number of economists operating in the Department of Finance as well as in the Department of Trade and Commerce and similar departments, so that in a small way and in a rather uncoordinated fashion the government is playing a role in the newer scientific field of social science research.
I bring this subject before the house tonight, Mr. Speaker, because as the motion stands there does not seem to be much opportunity for further consideration of this important aspect of research in Canada. The scope is going to be narrowed stringently indeed even though the senior hon. member for Halifax indicates that there will be opportunity for discussion of general research problems.


Unless we have the motion amended to provide for the calling of persons and papers the door will be pretty well shut to a consideration of the government role in social science research.
It would mean, for example, that there would not be the opportunity of calling in any representatives from our universities. Almost from time immemorial, universities have been the centre of creative activity in western civilization. I fail to see how it would be possible to deal adequately with research generally if we do not have the opportunity of calling before the committee some representatives of Canada's outstanding universities. It would be an extremely short-sighted policy indeed that would deny us this opportunity. Actually it would result in the work of the committee being almost fruitless.
Coming back now to the major emphasis I want to make tonight. While the government has done something in the realm of social science research, the voluntary groups have been much more active, particularly the Canadian social science research council. At the moment this council is faced with a rather difficult situation. Its traditional source of funds is drying up. Unfortunately Canada has depended largely upon United States foundations for the funds with which to carry on the important work of providing fellowships and scholarships at the graduate level in the area of social science. Each year recently the Canadian social science research council has been providing some 130 research fellowships. The money for those fellowships has come largely from two sources, namely the Rockefeller foundation and the Carnegie foundation. The Carnegie foundation, for example, has been contributing $90,000 annually. These contributions come to a total of some $8 million since it was first established in 1911. The Rockefeller foundation has been contributing $35,000 annually, and altogether a total of $12 million since it was established in 1914.
The Americans are becoming extremely reluctant to support Canadian research activity in this way. The difficulty first arose because of the report of the royal commission on the arts and sciences known as the Massey commission, which at that time was trying to encourage a more active participation on the part of the government and the people of Canada in our own social science research activity.
The introductory statements of the Massey commission said something to this effect: We have gained much from United States aid. In this preliminary stocktaking of Canadian cultural life it may be fair to inquire

whether we have gained a little too much. Granted that most of these United States donations are good in themselves, it does not follow that they have always been good for Canadians. We have not much right to be proud of our record as patrons of the arts. Is it possible that, besides the munificence of a Carnegie or a Rockefeller, Canadian contributions look so small that it seems hardly worth while making them? Or have we learned, wrongly, from our neighbour an unnecessary dependence on the contributions of the rich? Perhaps we have been tempted by a too-easy benevolence, but this leaves us in an undignified position, unworthy of our real power and prestige.
Now it seems that United States sources of support of the kind I have indicated took exception to the criticism of their contributions in this way. It was meant, of course, to be a prod to greater Canadian participation, but unfortunately it has had just the reverse effect. In the words of Blair Fraser, who was writing in Maclean's magazine last September 3 on this problem, the United States benefactors are now taking the attitude so far as Canada is concerned, you put up or shut up. Unfortunately there has been a very discouraging effect on the growing demands on the funds available from the voluntary Canadian social sciences research council.
In recent months there has been an attempt to influence Canadian industry, as well as the Canadian government of course, to meet the growing needs in the area of human relations. There has been no success as yet so far as the approach to the government is concerned because, as we know, no attempt has been made to implement the recommendations of the Massey commission in this regard. Last year the W. Burton Hurd memorial foundation was established, and a considerable effort was exerted to interest Canadian industrialists in making substantial contributions to this memorial fund.
Speaking personally, Mr. Speaker, I know of no more worthy name that could be associated with this fund. I see the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) looking at me. I think he came under the influence of Professor Burton Hurd in his days at Brandon College, back in the twenties when Brandon College was evidently turning out C.C.F.'ers. I came under the same influence in the thirties when the same institution was turning out Conservatives. Later Professor Hurd went to McMaster University where he chaired the department of political economy. His name, therefore, as one of Canada's outstanding economists, one of Canada's pioneers in the field of population
Committee on Atomic Energy studies, should have rallied enthusiastic support. Unfortunately it did not, and only $15,000 was realized through this effort. Unfortunately the money was not of the foundation type; it was not a continuing sum of money. It was a one contribution proposition only.
In this area of social science research, therefore, the situation is becoming extremely critical from the financial standpoint in the first instance, and also from the lack of co-ordinating effort to adjust to this obviously growing need. The government is moving gradually into the field in its various departments, but we are moving so slowly we are not even keeping pace, to use the phrase that the hon. member for Lambton West used this afternoon. As technological change increases as a result of the progress toward automation, we are going to be left far behind.
We are already behind in this matter of trying to gather the necessary information. We can only do that as the committee is permitted to bring before it people from the universities. Activity of this kind is largely confined to the universities. We can only get the necessary information concerning the needs and the action required if we are permitted to bring before the committee the men who are endeavouring to deal with the growing problem under the various circumstances and conditions I have outlined.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce gave us one argument for not agreeing to the amendment before us, the problem of guarding classified information. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that difficulty would be entirely removed if the revised amendment presented by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra is taken into consideration. I would certainly suggest that all hon. members should see their way clear to support this very important amendment.
One final word. I feel that in a committee of this kind we can only make a beginning in tackling the challenge of research. If it is going to be successful, if we are really going to meet the challenge of the changing situation, it should be a continuing committee, and we should have the opportunity each year of bringing ourselves up to date with the changing circumstances.

subsubtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN NON-MILITARY RESEARCH
speechtext:
Ordinarily, Mr. Speaker, I would not speak on a resolution to set up a committee. But since the amendment has been moved I think I have something to say on this particular subject. I am not posing as an expert on atomic energy or research. I do not suppose there are many in this house who could.
1726	HOUSE OF
Committee on Atomic Energy All we know about the subject is what we have read in the press, lectures we have heard and conversations we have had with people who have attempted to make a study of it.
I think the idea of setting up the committee is timely. I am not particularly concerned with the matter of national research, but I am concerned about the peaceful uses of atomic energy. If you once got into that subject in all its ramifications, you could talk a long time and perhaps get tangled up so badly you would not know where you were when you finished.
I am going to stick to one aspect of it, and that is this matter of radiation. The people of Canada, and perhaps the people of the world, require some assurance on that subject. Since 1945 we have heard many statements broadcast and there have been panel discussions on the subject of what atomic blasts are doing to the world. For quite a while people were jittery. Today they have become kind of apathetic. Since 1945, despite all of the warnings and so forth, nothing has happened here, although we did have the demonstration of the Japanese fishermen getting badly burned by the fall-out from an atomic explosion that took place a long way off. The matter is still being discussed. The time has come for the Canadian government to begin to get as much information as there is available on the subject for the purpose of reassuring our people that at least they are making some study of the matter.
Along with the hon. member for Bran-don-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale), and a couple of other hon. members, I had the pleasure of attending a portion of the last session of the United Nations under the capable leadership of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). When you go there as an observer you do not have any particular duties to perform. You have a free hand. You can sit in on any of the committees that are sitting, and also attend the general assembly when it is in session. As the hon. member for Brandon-Souris mentioned, at the last session of the United Nations the political committee talked at great length on this subject of the effects of radiation on genetics, and what radiation was going to do to the human race in the future. After sitting there day after day and listening to the discussions of men who are perhaps the best informed in the world on the subject, at least a little of it rubbed off on us. In addition, we did have the pleasure of meeting with the late Dr. Cipriani, who was an expert in that line at Chalk River, and we had discussions with him. It is unfortunate that a man of his age IMr. Gillis.l

and his knowledge and personality had to leave us at this time and take his knowledge with him.
You meet some people whom you never forget. He was that kind of person. He told us a lot about this particular subject. He was the kind of person who does not use the technical language that is used by some people. He seemed to be the kind of person who could get down to where you were and talk to you in understandable language. I gathered from what I heard in that committee, and from what the late Dr. Cipriani had to say privately on the subject, that not much is known about the effects of radiation.
There always has been a certain build-up of radiation in the world. That build-up takes place to a greater extent in some countries than in others. I think I am correct in saying it was mentioned that the north of Scotland had a higher radiation build-up than any other section of the world. The Scandinavian countries, and I suppose British Columbia, would have a higher build-up than the prairies. There always has been a build-up in radiation. You get it from many things.
Dr. Cipriani's judgment was that it was difficult to say very much right now as to whether or not it was building up to the danger point, for the simple reason that there is no data on it. No formula has been perfected by the different countries as to how to get a uniform measurement. Each country was using a different formula, with the result that what one country was doing could not be compared with what another country was doing. The committee's job was to try to set up an atomic energy agency that would function within the structure of United Nations.
Of course there was difficulty for a long time in getting it set up because every time the matter of radiation measurements and that kind of thing came up they had their opposition there also. The opposition would appear with a bombshell and say, "We must discontinue the blasts for a long time".
They finally agreed on setting up an agency. It has been set up. The scientists of the world have formed a committee. That committee is either meeting now or will meet shortly. The hon. member for Brandon-Souris says it is meeting now. Their objective is to get some data on the radiation build-up that has taken place in the world since the discharge of the atomic and hydrogen bombs. Until that agency gets proper measurements that will be comparable in every section of the world I do not think anybody can say anything with any authority

as to what the situation is today with respect to radiation and genetics. That data is not available.
Now is a good time lor the Canadian government to demonstrate to our people that we are interested in this particular subject. Perhaps the Minister ol Trade and Commerce was quite correct when he objected to the first amendment and said that classified material that was on the secret list should not be made public. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has amended his amendment and is now asking only for the right to call witnesses and have unclassified material; that is, material that is not on the secret list, which he thinks should be made available. I do not think there is much on the secret list today, anyway.
I am supporting the amendment because I think it is necessary that we should begin to tell our people that we are making an active study of the subject.
While attending the United Nations session I was impressed with what the United States was doing in this field. For example, for three weeks at least while I was there they had a display of all the equipment that is used in the atomic energy field in the Carnegie building just across from the United Nations building. They took the uranium right from the ore state and traced it down to the splitting of the atom. Every machine that is used in any of these plants was there in miniature form operating exactly as it operates in a real plant. They had a capable man on each machine to tell exactly what the function of the machine was. There was a lot of equipment there, because it took me exactly three hours to go through the display and get a little idea of what each of the machines was doing and of the possibilities of the atom in the future in a peaceful way.
I was amazed to find the things you can do with that material today. In the development of agriculture, for example, there was a demonstration of what it will do for wheat and the many ways it can improve it. We were shown how perishable foods are preserved; but the thing that impressed me most were the possibilities of the atom for medicinal purposes, for health purposes. There was a demonstration showing the improvement in the X-ray machine and the use of isotopes in determining what is wrong with the human body. There is no guess work any more with the new equipment they have in the X-ray field and with the use of the isotopes for determining what is wrong with the body. According to the lecture I heard there is no guess work any more. This new equipment shows every tissue in the human
Committee on Atomic Energy body; it shows what is going on. The technician can tell the doctor what is wrong.
They tell me that most of the large hospitals in New York are equipped with that type of equipment. It is very expensive and it is scarce at the present time, but they assured us it would not be far in the future until most of the larger centres will be furnished with that kind of equipment. If we are sensible, and I think from all indications we are now learning how to live together in the world through fear, if through nothing else, we can put the atom to use for peaceful purposes. If we do that, the possibilities are unlimited.
My understanding is that the government of the United States has provided all that equipment. It must have cost a lot of money. They put on that demonstration, as I understand it, at Geneva and then they took the equipment over to the last session of the United Nations for all to see. If I had seen nothing else, my trip to New York was worth while because of that demonstration and the possibilities it illustrated of the use of the atom for peace in the future.
I think we are missing the boat when our government is not keeping as closely as possible in touch with that kind of thing and showing our people the possibility of using this atom, which is scaring everyone today because of the possibilities of war, for peaceful purposes. We should be playing up the constructive uses of the atom and playing down the idea of war. As I said before, I think we will have peace for some considerable time through fear; but in order to guarantee that peace we should harness the machine that can be used for destruction and put it to the constructive uses I have mentioned; and we should gain the support of the Canadian people and people throughout the world for the constructive use of the atom.
For the reasons I have mentioned I am supporting the amendment. I believe it is right to set up a committee; but in addition to having a committee I believe it should be able to call in men from the Department of External Affairs and men from the atomic energy plant at Chalk River who would be able to tell the committee what is being done by other governments and what our government is doing to co-operate with other countries in this field.
We are not disseminating enough of that kind of information. I think we could make a start with this committee if we accepted the amendment that has been moved by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. That is my main purpose in rising, Mr. Speaker, and I suggest to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, now that the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has moved his amendment

Committee on Atomic Energy and has pretty well specified what he needs in the way of evidence and documents, the acceptance of his amendment.
As the hon. member has said, anything that might be secret would be off the official list. Our acceptance of his amendment would probably shorten this debate. It would be good business if the minister would accept the amended resolution and let us get the committee set up and get down to business.

subsubtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN NON-MILITARY RESEARCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to mention a phase of research which I think should be covered by this committee. It is a field that means a great deal to a large number of Canadians, and it is a field which is apt to be overlooked. I refer to the general fisheries research field which should be considered by this proposed committee.
For authority to consider fisheries under this motion I would think that part (b) of the operations of the national research council would be sufficient. Section 7 of the Research Council Act, chapter 239 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, states, and I quote just the last part of the section, Mr. Speaker:
The council . . . also has the duty of advising the committee on questions of scientific and technological methods affecting the expansion of Canadian industries or the utilization of the natural resources of Canada.
The role of the federal government in fisheries generally is a matter of constitutional charter, but I think it would be sufficient to state that section 91, subsection 12 of the British North America Act, which gives -the federal authority the right to regulate and limit sea coast and inland fisheries would be enough authority here, with the exception of course that the provinces still retain provincial and civil rights in regard to fisheries.
I would hope that the powers of the committee, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has suggested in his amendment, would include the right to call for all papers- those would be unclassified papers-and persons and records.
There is generally a new interest in the exploration of the sea. A few years ago it was all air but today, with the increasing interest we find in the sea, we read of the frogmen in the deep, underwater television and all these new ideas concerning the ocean depths. This brings to mind the potentialities of this seemingly small but important fishing industry that has no strong lobbying power and no great industry upon which it can rely for subsidy and assistance in research. Nevertheless it is an important factor in our future.
In order to begin I ask the question, just what is being done now in fisheries research?
[Mr. Gillis.l
I am pleased to report that as far as I can see personally we are making very good progress in this particular field. As the Minister of Fisheries recently said-and I must admit that the Minister of Fisheries is research conscious-when he addressed the Fisheries Council of Canada on January 4, with the commissions and other bodies today it is necessary to keep up and continue research in all branches of fisheries.
Recently I had some questions and answers tabled with regard to the money that is spent by the government on fisheries products in relation to the total market value. If my quick arithmetic serves me well I think it is fair to say that on fisheries research we are spending between one-half and three-quarters of 1 per cent of the total market landed value of our fisheries. This is comparatively good, I think, but like everything else it can be better, and I suggest that further stimulation needs to be given to fisheries research and perhaps better coordination.
What would be some of the problems into which this committee could inquire regarding fisheries research? I suggest that there would be the small problems that are encountered from day to day, such as the problems of lobster fishing and of the seasons, all of which have to be looked into. Last year we had the unusual circumstance of herring cluttering up the lobster traps due to a peculiar condition which caused their death. This was a matter that required scientific investigation. When the results came out it was found that this particular heart condition affecting the herring was depleting the lobsters.
Then there is the problem in connection with clams and green crabs which is causing so much trouble. The clam industry goes back to the days of Champlain, when he found it necessary to rely on these lovely, delicious clams to help sustain life in the early days in Canada.
There is another problem which is a continuing one, and which the Minister of Fisheries has said presents one of the greatest challenges to the department. I refer to the decline in salmon production. This is a field which deserves considerable attention. According to information which has been tabled, the value of research in this connection has been made clear and I admit that the figures given are good when considered in relation to the total value of the salmon catch. But we are getting nowhere as far as the salmon industry is concerned.
As far as the situation in New Brunswick is concerned, there are said to be four or five reasons for this decline in salmon production. First there is the industrialization,

which is inevitable. Then there is the spruce budworm, which brings in the Department of Agriculture. There has been a conflict of statements in this regard. Some research experts say that the spruce budworm has had no effect upon salmon production, while others say that it has had a direct effect. I believe the fisheries research authorities have said that this spraying has been going on for only a few years and that the cycle of salmon growth will not have been completed for one or two more years, and that therefore definite conclusions cannot be reached in this respect.
This is a problem for our research experts, and I submit that this committee should satisfy itself that such problems are looked into. If this were done we might be able to reverse the serious decline of 66 per cent which has taken place in our salmon industry from 1930 to the present time. Japan has shown the way in recent years. By the use of modern research methods they have been able to triple their salmon output.
Having said that, I come to the third question. What could be done in this fisheries research field? There are many solutions for the problems confronting the salmon industry, but one that comes quickly to my mind is the successful efforts which have been made to hurry the growth of young trout and salmon. This biological discovery was made by chance by a fisheries expert in the mari-times, whose name I think was Kenneth Shillington. He found that by segregating hardy types of salmon and trout he could increase their growth as much as one pound a year. If this discovery is fostered and promoted by our experts it should prove a quick solution to the problem that confronts both the commercial fisherman and the angler.
Further research work should be done in connection with lobsters, in the use of the new steel traps and in other ways. Coming to clams again, this problem is more of a technological nature, in the development of new diggers and other efficient methods of fishing.
If this committee finds it feasible to call in the fisheries experts there are two questions which should be foremost in their minds. First there is the biological inquiry that should be made. Most fisheries experts will agree that we have to consider the life of the sea from a strictly biological point of view. What is that life like? Where does it exist? In what parts of the sea will it be found? Ocean currents, temperature and the like all have to be considered.
After this fundamental biological knowledge has been taken into account and the complete
Committee on Atomic Energy life history and environment of the particular fish ascertained, then we would be prepared to consider the second or technological aspect. That of course would take in the complete life of the fish up to its eventual delivery to market.
In this connection I think we should consider what has been done in this field in other countries, and I would refer in particular to legislation passed in the United States on July 1, 1954. While this legislation might not be completely feasible for Canada, it has provided co-ordination and stimulus for the fishing industry in that country. This legislation is commonly known as the Salton-stall-Kennedy act and was the result of successful lobbying by Messrs. Saltonstall and Kennedy. The legislation provided that the department of the interior, under which fisheries comes, would receive 30 per cent of all tariffs obtained from the import of fish products. The pertinent part of this legislation which I intend to quote will give an idea of what my theme is this evening. The act was set up:
(1)	to promote the free flow of domestically produced fishery products in commerce by conducting a fishery educational service and fishery technological, biological and related research programs, the moneys so transferred to be also available for the purchase or other acquisition, construction, equipment, operation, and maintenance of vessels or other facilities necessary for conducting research as provided for in this section, and
(2)	to develop and increase markets for fishery products of domestic origin and (3) to conduct any biological, technological, or other research pertaining to American fisheries.
In the report of this committee a further significant matter was brought out. That is the fact that this legislation in itself did not provide everything. It was a fact that when the legislation was being lobbied, promoted and discussed in the United States it was necessary to set up committees and call in experts in the various biological and technical fields of the fisheries industry to make their statements and offer their independent suggestions as to the future of the industry. That should be the lesson of this legislation for us. It was not enough in itself; it had to have the expert stimulation that was so necessary.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I should like to review the thoughts I have expressed. I pointed out that I believe the committee should consider research into the fishing industry in as detailed fashion as possible. We should inquire what is being done. I suggested that our fisheries research in Canada is good. However, it has to be better because we have a small new industry and continual promotion is essential. Having said

Committee on Atomic Energy that, I dealt with one or two problems into which inquiry should be made. I suggested what could be done, what might be put before the experts or what the experts might do to help the industry. Finally, 1 mentioned the Saltonstall-Kennedy legislation. I think we should definitely take note of it and, if it is within the powers of the committee, invite an expert who has dealt with this matter in the New England states to appear before the committee.
I call for greater emphasis on and greater investment in this necessary part of our industrial life in Canada. The fishing industry is so essential to both coasts of this country that we should be certain it is given due promotion. We must always remember that the economy of the maritimes is lagging, and the fishing industry is lagging within that economy. I hope that this committee, with amended powers, will take note of my plea for the necessary consideration of an important phase of our industrial life.

subsubtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN NON-MILITARY RESEARCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was one of those who urged last session that such a committee be set up then. I urged it on the basis of a rather important statement made by President Eisenhower of the United States. The committee was not set up last year; unfortunately it did not function. However, we are happy to support the setting up of the committee this year, and also to support the amendment that has been moved providing for the calling of persons and papers.
In reading the resolution closely I find that the most pertinent part of it, as far as I can see, is that which refers to the role of government. The motion reads:
That a special committee be appointed to examine into the role of government in the field of nonmilitary research in Canada, including:
(a)	operations in the field of atomic energy,
(b)	operations of the national research council.
I hope I have not read the motion incorrectly, but as I read it, it does not really call for the setting up of a committee to examine the operations in the field of atomic energy or the operations of the national research council proper. Rather it calls for an examination of the part the government should play in these matters. I do not know how extensive its work would be, and I am suggesting that perhaps the Minister of Trade and Commerce overlooked that point.
If we take the resolution literally, any examination into the field of atomic energy itself or into the operations of the national research council could possibly be ruled out. The chairman of the committee could say that we are not concerned with these things, that all we are concerned about is the role


the government is going to play in them, whether it is going to enter into these fields or whether it is not, whether the government should take over the results of the work of the national research council and run the whole show of atomic production, or whether that should be left to private enterprise.
I trust that is not the intention of the government and the actual meaning of the wording of the resolution. I take it, and I am sure the house is under the impression, that the actual meaning is that the committee can examine into all questions covering operation in the field of atomic energy and concerning the national research council. I point that out because I do not want anything to happen once the committee is set up.
Reading the resolution again, I refer to the pertinent point, the role of government. I suppose everyone knows what the word "role" means. I thought I did, but for the sake of making sure I sent for an English dictionary. I find that the first definition given here is "actor's part". I hope the government is going to be a little more than an actor in some drama, because usually actors are sort of fictitious individuals who portray a good deal of unreality. However, the definition continues and says, "One's function". I think that is the definition that is meant by the role of government, what the function of government should be with respect to these various fields of research.
In anything a committee does, Mr. Speaker, in anything parliament does, in anything the government does, and with respect to all laws passed in this house, I am sure we should have one particular objective in mind. I believe we have reason to ask one pertinent question, particularly when it comes to the discussion of the work of this committee. As those who are responsible for the eventual destiny of the nation, I think the one over-all and fundamental question that we have to deal with is this: What is the purpose of life? In the matter of this resolution, I do not think we should look at it with the idea of seeing, for instance, how a corporation that enters into the business of atomic energy could make a million dollars. Rather I think we should look to see how, through the discoveries that are made and the development of these sciences, the nation can reach that ultimate objective of a full life.
When we begin to think of the subject in those terms I fancy several extremely important factors are brought into operation. The first one I am going to speak of is this, and here I ask another question. We should ask ourselves this question: What are we

able to do in the realm of physical or material sciences to reach the objective which I have already stated, namely the full and abundant life for the Canadian people? We have now reached an age when, in the material sense, nothing seems to be impossible. Through scientific ventures we seem to be able to do almost anything which the human mind conceives.
We now talk of the discovery of atomic energy. We perhaps think of this energy as a new thing, but it will not be too long, perhaps within the space of a generation, until we shall be talking of another new type of energy, namely solar energy. As the nation progresses, one thing displaces another. Before we get atomic energy to a place where it is recognized and used by the nation, it may become almost obsolete overnight through the advent of solar energy.
There is another matter I believe the committee and the government should take into account when we are thinking of research into all these modern sciences, and it is this. What do we produce these modern appliances for? What do we produce anything for? Is it not for the good of the people? Do we not investigate these various fields of science with a view to bringing into operation the result, whatever the case may be, for the benefit of the people of the country? Is that always done?
While I believe that private industry is playing its normal part and perhaps more in these matters, I am wondering whether private industry recognizes its purpose. Is the purpose of private industry to make millions? Is that the ultimate purpose? Of course if we live in a dollar complex and simply say, "It is the purpose of life to build up a fortune", then we are just missing the object of life. The purpose of industry is to produce, and the purpose of production is to satisfy the requirements of the nation.
Let us consider this field of research. For instance, I am told that we can produce steel so hard that it will never wear out. I am told that. I read that in various journals that come to my desk. Then I ask the question: Are these things that are built of steel built to be used? Are they built for permanency? Let us consider the automobile. It is possible to manufacture an automobile of steel that will never wear out. Why do we not do it? The reason is that when they manufacture an automobile, they manufacture it for the purpose of it wearing out. The same is true with regard to anything else. As my friend the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) says, it is the same with the electric light bulb. I fancy they could manufacture a light bulb that would burn forever,
Committee on Atomic Energy or burn for a lifetime. Why do we not do it then? The reason is that eventually, if we do that, we shall come to a place where industry will be slowed down.
Let us look at the matter fairly and squarely. Suppose it is slowed down. Even today we find that labour is beginning to recognize that problem and say, "We will do things now by working 30 hours a week instead of 40 hours". Suppose that is so. What about it? Suppose we can do these things by working 10 hours a week. What about it? Why not? Let us go on a holiday for the rest of the week. Why not? If the function of an economic system is to produce an abundant living, why not? I think this consideration enters the picture, namely that industry, in the course of economic events, must get back its investment before the new can displace the old.

subsubtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN NON-MILITARY RESEARCH
speechtext:
As you
have just reminded the house, Mr. Speaker, we are considering the setting up of a committee to examine into and report on the role of government in research matters. This proposed committee could be one of great benefit and far-reaching significance. How well it does its work, and how well it can do its work, seems to depend to some extent on its powers. We have that secondary issue before us by way of an amendment.
It seems to me that this committee should have a scope which permits it to go beyond the hearing of evidence from those now engaged in scientific research in the various agencies of the federal government, and to call from industry and the academic world from all parts of Canada people who are able to contribute advice or information which the committee will need if it is to give any clear lead as to what is the proper role of government. I believe we all concede the importance of research, and I need not dwell on that. We also recognize the government's need of advice which can be obtained through the instrumentality of a committee such as this.
The federal government is not the only government to set up a committee of this kind, or to obtain assistance from advisory sources. I refer to the advisory committee on scientific policy which has been performing similar functions for the government of the United Kingdom. I should like to indicate my view of the importance of what is done in the field of research by quoting from the seventh
IMr. Hansell.l

annual report of this United Kingdom committee. It makes this very significant summary:
Today a country's wealth and power are largely determined by the extent of its scientific knowledge and by its capacity to use that knowledge.
To me that means a country's standard of living and its capacity to defend itself. A country's wealth and power is largely determined by the extent of its scientific knowledge and its capacity to use that knowledge. Those are the issues on which the government wants assistance from this committee.
I suggest that the importance of research and scientific knowledge is such that the government cannot afford to be wrong if it is to keep Canada in its proper place amongst the nations of the world. At the moment there is no single agency which has the oversight of all the multifarious research activities in which people engage, some under the aegis of the government and some under provincial and industrial direction. There is no single agency today which is in a position to oversee the entire field and give the advice which this committee will be asked to give. It is true that there are a great many agencies, and we all know the more important of them. One of them is the national research council, but even it does not cover the whole field and is not in the position which this committee will be to review and advise the government on its proper role.
Perhaps there is a parallel here between the C.B.C., which is actually engaged in broadcasting as well as regulating broadcasting, and the sort of supervisory commission which has been suggested as necessary and desirable to regulate the C.B.C. and the private agencies. This committee would stand above the national research council and look over not only its work but other research activity in the country in which the federal government could possibly be interested.
Another agency of the federal government, as is well known, is the committee on scientific research of the privy council, comprising six or seven ministers under whose direction the national research council functions. Then we have the research branches of the various departments of government, beginning with agriculture which has been engaged in this field the longest, and running through mines, the board of grain commissioners under the Department of Trade and Commerce, fisheries and some other departments which have fairly substantial research branches. Then we have the universities. We have industrial laboratories, some engaged in very extensive research such as that done by the pulp and paper companies.

Then we go on to agencies under provincial jurisdiction. Alberta has a research council. There was a research council in Ontario, and there is the Ontario research foundation today. As I have said, there is a multitude of agencies now working toward the desirable end of applying scientific knowledge to the good of Canadians and the Canadian life.
I think I might illustrate the problem which is before the house by referring to the experience which the Ontario government had seven or eight years ago when, under the leadership of the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), who was then premier of Ontario, they set up a commission under the public inquiries act which had almost the same terms of reference as are suggested for this select committee of the house. It was to consider what was the proper role of the provincial government in this field of research; where it could properly spend money in research and where it should not, and how its responsibilities could be correlated with those of the federal and other authorities so there would not be overlapping, and all would be integrated for the greatest usefulness. That commission, under its terms of reference, recommended legislation under which an advisory council was formed and functioned for several years with the sole purpose of assisting the government in determining how far it should go in spending public funds on research.
If I may refer to that Ontario commission briefly, the first task it undertook and recommended was that of providing more trained personnel through scholarships, something which the federal government is now doing on a more extensive scale through the national research council scholarships, which were paid out in the sum of something over $600,000 last year. Ontario research scholarships in the amount of $50,000 annually have provided advanced training, post-graduate training, for a number of people who are now available for scientific research. It is obvious that the basis of research is the people who are trained to do it.
That was the first proper role of government which was recommended. Then the council set about co-ordinating the work of federal, provincial and private agencies through advisory committees which were established, one in each of seven or eight important fields, such as the advisory committee on agriculture and the one on fisheries and wildlife. I believe that similar advisory committees have been usefully serving the national research council.
These committees bring together at one time and place and several times during the year all the men and women who are engaged
Committee on Atomic Energy in a specific type of research, where they exchange experiences and learn what each other is doing and avoid in that way the duplication which is so easy and so wasteful in the scientific field where there is so much to be done.
Then there were grants in aid of specific research, and so on. That effort to obtain proper advice is a parallel to what we are doing here today. The complication which exists because of the federal nature of our government is one of the problems that make it particularly necessary that such a committee should review periodically the role of government. There has to be not only the co-ordination of the federal government activities with those of industry, private institutions and universities, but the provinces also have a jurisdiction. There is the problem of integrating the research expenditures and work of eleven governments that operate in their own fields.
Another difficulty which may arise from the reference which is made in this resolution is the distinction between civil and military research. The resolution limits the committee to inquiring into non-military research in Canada! It may not be easy to say what is non-military. A very interesting example came to my attention the other day. There are two researchers, Dr. K. C. Fisher and Donald Smith, who are doing research in the Arctic area on a very humble little animal known as the lemming. I do not recall the hon. member for Mackenzie River (Mr. Har-die) mentioning this animal among his pets in the very interesting address he gave the other night; but the lemming is a celebrated animal in the Arctic which, according to tradition, is reputed to commit mass suicide by rushing into the sea and drowning itself.
There are two university professors looking into this matter at the expense of the federal government under the defence research council; therefore it is a military type of research. They are trying to find out how the lemming lives in that cold climate and whether he does or does not drown himself en masse. They are trying to find out all about the lemming. It is a very interesting piece of research. The suicide theory has been exploded, and I expect that in the long run some very useful information for civilians who live and work in the north country may come out of this. I mention it simply to point out the difficulty in trying to draw a clear line between what is civilian and what is military in the research field.
I am sure this committee will not be circumscribed in inquiring into matters which are on the borderline, as everyone has freely agreed it should not have the authority to

If the committee proceeds with full power,
I suggest that some of its likely subjects of recommendation are, first, the field of the actual doing of research, which is part of the work of the national research council today. It is engaged in carrying out actual specific research projects, and in very substantial numbers. This is a proper role of government.
In Ontario, the Ontario research foundation does that same kind of work. It is a co-operative effort of government and industry, the capital having been put up some years ago by the two, with industry subscribing part of the capital and the government the remainder. It is a custom researcher. It receives orders from industry and carries them out, and gives the answers where it can and charges a fee. I daresay that is the method under which the national research council carries on some of its work. This is one proper role of government, the actual doing of research.
Then a second role is that of sponsoring research by others, either by financial grants in aid, or in the case of industry I should think probably by matching similar contributions by industry. In the case of universities, very extensive research is carried on today under grants from the federal government as well as from the provincial governments, and that is a proper role of government.
Then there is the problem of co-ordination of the work among the various agencies I have mentioned. The committee will undoubtedly have something to say about that if it does its job well.
The most important role of government is to make known the results of useful research when those results have been obtained, because after all the application of scientific knowledge gained through research to the ordinary affairs of life is what creates the wealth and power to which I referred earlier in this speech.
There is one other matter which is also of considerable importance, and that is the problem of utilizing the scientific personnel and facilities of the country to the best advantage. As I said, there is a limited number of people and limited facilities, and this committee could properly inquire into the use of those limited facilities.
Finally there is the question of providing more personnel. It seems to me that this is one of the most important problems which this committee could consider. We all know that as soon as an engineer gets his diploma from a university today he is offered a job

subsubtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN NON-MILITARY RESEARCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join with my colleagues on all sides of the house in welcoming the formation of this committee to undertake an examination into the role of government in the field of non-military research. I do hope, however, that the Minister of Trade and Commerce will accede to the request embodied in the amendment to the resolution moved by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. That amendment as further amended at eight o'clock would give this committee authority to send for persons and unclassified papers and records.
The minister did make a case, I think, as regards classified records or documents. I do not think any hon. member of the house would want to have any part in running any danger of making available information of a classified or secret nature. I believe, however, the amendment with the restriction as to papers and records being only those which are unclassified would certainly get around that problem.
As for the matter of sending for persons, the minister suggested it was possible that persons who are concerned with the government in the field of atomic research or the operations of the research council might inadvertently let loose some classified information if they were being examined by members of that committee. I think if individuals in the government service can be trusted to the extent of having access to classified information, we can certainly trust their discretion not to reveal information of a classified nature in appearances before a committee such as is proposed. I therefore hope that the minister will accede to the amendment as amended.
There is one phase of the operation of this committee which I think is quite important. Outside of the field of government activities, atomic energy research and national research council research, we have the problem of the role of government in encouraging and assisting research undertaken by industry generally, in other words
Committee on Atomic Energy by private interests. I hope this committee will have the opportunity to examine most fully the policies of the government through an examination of members of the government and members of the proper government departments as to the policies and procedures being followed by the government in encouraging private enterprise, corporations or industries to undertake a larger part of the job of essential non-military research in Canada.
Very obviously a good part of the government's role in private research is involved in the operations and the policies of the income tax department. I believe that much more could be done by the government through income tax concessions in various forms to encourage private industry to itself undertake a greater measure of essential research. I also believe the government could encourage industry to stimulate purely creative research backed by industry by allowing as credits for income tax purposes, in other words the deduction from taxable income, grants to foundations, universities and scholarships awarded by corporations or industries to universities in order to further stimulate the broad field of research in industry in Canada.
One side effect, and an important one, of any expanded research program in Canada, both that undertaken by private industry and that undertaken by the government, would be in effect a measure of conservation of one of Canada's most vital resources. I refer, of course, to the research brains developed in Canada. There should be provided in Canada opportunities for our research brains to undertake creative employment within Canada in all phases of industry, and thus slow up the migration of a good part of our Canadian-produced talent to the United States and elsewhere in the world where the opportunities for research are greater than they are in Canada today.
In the few moments that remain before ten o'clock I should like to speak briefly about one or two phases of research in the hydrocarbon field which, of course, is of considerable interest to western Canada where we have such huge reserves of all forms of hydrocarbons. We have something like 40 billion tons of coal, and in the bitumen sands there is estimated to be something between 100 and 300 billion barrels of liquid bitumen. Then there are our vast resources of crude oil and natural gas.
In connection with the tar sands there has been co-operative research by government and industry for a good many years. This research has been in the usage of the tar

Those tar sands constitute for Canada and for the world resources of almost limitless magnitude for the centuries ahead, when the more conventional types'of oil may be depleted.
For many years the national research council has undertaken extensive research into better methods of separating the bitumen from the sand, and so has the Alberta research council. During the last world war and for some years afterwards private industry undertook similar research. In the last year or two there have been some new developments.
A rather interesting one occurred more or less by accident. A man who was not a trained researcher, who was not a trained chemist or an engineer, carried out some experiments in the basement of his home in Calgary to determine some simple means of separating the bitumen wrapped around the grains of these tar sands of northern Alberta. By accident he finally hit on something which has considerable promise.
He found that if the bituminous sand was mixed with kerosene and then put through a centrifuge with cold, salty water there would be brought about a separation of the bitumen and the sand. In the last two years some hundreds of thousands of dollars have been spent by private groups in an effort to turn this idea into an economically feasible method of separation of the bitumen and the sand.
Research is being carried a little further in an effort to develop more efficient and more economical means of mining these huge beds of bitumen sands in northern Alberta. Research is being carried on to a limited extent in connection with the next problem of what to do with the bitumen once it has been mined and separated from the sands.
There is a big field for the future in which government and private industry can spend not only a great deal of money but effort and time in the hope of arriving at a solution of the great problem of turning these tremendous natural resources into something that can be used for the good of this country.
In connection with coal there has been a great deal of research both in Canada and elsewhere in the world. Coal is now being turned into a great many products used by mankind. Some of our women are now wearing clothes made from coal, and there is a whole host of medicines derived from coal. Cosmetics and a full range of other products in everyday use are derived from the basic

product of black coal. The national research council has done a great deal of fine work in the development of coal-fired gas turbines, and research at McGill University has accomplished a great deal in that regard as well. This is a field of research which if continued to an effective conclusion should open up new prospects for one of Canada's depressed industries, the coal industry of the maritimes and the prairies.
Until a few years ago natural gas was considered a waste by-product of oil, but in the last two decades gas has become not only a fuel but a major raw material for the production of a whole host of chemical and petrochemical products. For example, during the last war natural gas which had been going to waste in the Turner valley field near Calgary, at a place called Hell's Half Acre, was used to produce munitions for the allied war effort. Natural gas combined with air provided the means of making munitions. That particular wartime plant near Calgary is now in operation combining the components of natural gas with the components of air to turn out fertilizers. The ammonia plant is now playing a most important part in the economy of that community, and is providing a sizeable portion of the chemical fertilizers being used in this country, with considerable left for export.
This procedure of turning gas and oil into a host of products has resulted from research. Today many products are being produced from hydrocarbons which are found in abundance in many parts of Canada. As an instance we have the gas, a petroleum byproduct, which provides the artificial rubbers being produced by the Polymer Corporation at Sarnia, and then we have everything from fertilizers, medicinal products, clothing and a whole range of chemicals that are now being produced. In the years to come there will be a long list of all sorts of products which will help to make Canada and the world a better place in which to live.
On motion of Mr. Nickle the debate was adjourned.
